articles.title: Mianmar chama de ‘injusta’ decisão da Corte da ONU sobre genocídio de rohingyas | G1
articles.standfirst: Corte Internacional de Justiça concluiu que forças de segurança do país cometeram genocídio contra a minoria muçulmana em 2017. Governo criticou placar de 9 a 6 entre os juízes.
articles.summary: Corte Internacional de Justiça concluiu que forças de segurança do país cometeram genocídio contra a minoria muçulmana em 2017. Governo criticou placar de 9 a 6 entre os juízes.
articles.body:
Muçulmanos rohingya, que cruzaram a fronteira de Myanmar para Bangladesh, estendem os braços para receber alimentos distribuídos por agências de ajuda humanitária perto do campo de refugiados de Balukhali, Bangladesh. — Foto: Dar Yasin/Associated Press

O governo de Mianmar classificou nesta sexta-feira (20) como “injusta” a decisão da Corte Internacional de Justiça que responsabilizou o país por genocídio contra a minoria muçulmana rohingya.

O julgamento foi divulgado na quinta-feira (19). Por 9 votos a 6, os juízes concluíram que Mianmar cometeu genocídio contra os rohingyas durante uma violenta operação militar realizada em 2017.

A porta-voz do presidente Min Aung Hlaing, Khine Khine Soe, afirmou a jornalistas na capital, Naypyitaw, que a falta de unanimidade entre os 15 juízes demonstraria, na avaliação do governo, que a sentença foi injusta.

“Nem todos os 15 juízes concordaram com a decisão, não foi uma decisão unânime. Eu diria que foi injusta”, afirmou a porta-voz.

A reação é a primeira manifestação do governo de Mianmar após a decisão histórica da Corte.

A Corte Internacional de Justiça, principal tribunal da ONU, decidiu que os milhares de assassinatos e a violência sexual generalizada cometidos pelas forças de segurança de Mianmar contra os rohingyas em 2017 configuraram genocídio patrocinado pelo Estado.

Segundo a decisão, as ações tiveram a “intenção de destruir” uma parte substancial da população rohingya no norte do estado de Rakhine.

O tribunal concluiu que as forças de segurança mataram milhares de civis rohingyas, cometeram violência sexual generalizada, praticaram atos de extrema violência contra crianças e atacaram integrantes da minoria que tentavam fugir.

Refugiados rohingya participam de um comício com o discurso do presidente da Assembleia Geral das Nações Unidas, Khalilur Rahman, após o veredicto da Corte Internacional de Justiça de que Mianmar cometeu genocídio contra os rohingya , em um campo de refugiados em Cox's Bazar, Bangladesh. — Foto: Mohammad Ponir Hossain/Reuters

A Corte também determinou que Mianmar deve compensar os rohingyas pelas violações cometidas. Os valores das indenizações serão estabelecidos posteriormente.

Além disso, o país deverá permitir o“retorno seguro e digno” dos deslocados aos locais onde viviam e possibilitar a reunificação das famílias separadas.

A decisão é definitiva e não pode ser contestada.

10 mil rohingyas serão reassentados na Turquia

A manifestação de Mianmar ocorre no mesmo dia em que a Malásia anunciou que 10 mil refugiados rohingyas serão reassentados na Turquia.

O programa prevê capacitação profissional e será realizado em parceria com autoridades turcas, o Acnur e outras agências. A iniciativa foi anunciada um dia depois do reconhecimento do genocídio pela Corte.

Um grupo da minoria étnica Rohingya de Myanmar caminha por campos de arroz após cruzar a fronteira para Bangladesh perto da área de Teknaf, em Cox's Bazar. — Foto: Bernat Armangue/Associated Press

A Malásia tem cerca de 193 mil refugiados registrados de Mianmar, sendo aproximadamente dois terços deles rohingyas.

O governo malaio afirmou que a iniciativa de reassentamento busca uma solução de longo prazo para a situação dos refugiados no país e que a experiência poderá servir de modelo de cooperação entre países.

articles.title: Meta vê emissões subirem 45% e reavalia meta climática | G1
articles.standfirst: Expansão da IA exige mais centros de dados e põe em xeque compromisso de zerar emissões até 2030.
articles.summary: Expansão da IA exige mais centros de dados e põe em xeque compromisso de zerar emissões até 2030.
articles.body:
CEO da Meta, Mark Zuckerberg, experimenta os óculos inteligentes da Meta. — Foto: Carlos Barria/Reuters

A Meta, controladora de Facebook, Instagram e WhatsApp, informou nesta quinta-feira (19) que está reavaliando sua meta de alcançar a neutralidade de carbono até 2030 diante da expansão da inteligência artificial (IA).

Com isso, a empresa se junta a grandes corporações que vêm revendo seus compromissos relacionados ao combate ao aquecimento global.

Em 2020, a Meta estabeleceu a meta de atingir emissões líquidas zero de carbono para se alinhar ao Acordo de Paris, que busca limitar o aquecimento global de longo prazo a 1,5°C e evitar catástrofes climáticas.

"Estamos reavaliando nossos prazos, a sequência e os marcos intermediários, incluindo o horizonte de 2030 para nossa meta de emissões líquidas zero", afirmaram Rachel Peterson, vice-presidente de data centers, e Blair Swedeen, responsável global pela neutralidade de carbono da empresa, no relatório anual de sustentabilidade da companhia.

A Meta informou que suas emissões líquidas de carbono aumentaram 45% em 2025, alcançando 11,8 milhões de toneladas métricas. O cálculo é baseado em métodos de medição vistos com ceticismo por defensores do clima.

"Quando definimos nossa meta de emissões líquidas zero, prevíamos crescimento constante, redução dos custos da energia limpa e mudanças sistêmicas que permitiriam avançar no ritmo planejado. A realidade tem sido muito mais complexa", escreveram os executivos.

A expansão da inteligência artificial colocou esses compromissos em xeque. O desenvolvimento da tecnologia impulsionou uma corrida pela construção de centros de armazenamento de dados, que consomem grandes quantidades de energia e água.

A Meta afirmou que, para cumprir sua missão, "precisa construir a infraestrutura que sustenta a IA".

Neste ano, a empresa também abandonou um compromisso assumido com outras grandes multinacionais de utilizar exclusivamente eletricidade proveniente de fontes renováveis.

articles.title: Faltar ao trabalho por causa da cólica: quando a dor vira um alerta | G1
articles.standfirst: Agenda, estudos e convivência com a família: quando a dor dita a rotina, ela merece investigação, e não resignação.
articles.summary: Agenda, estudos e convivência com a família: quando a dor dita a rotina, ela merece investigação, e não resignação.
articles.body:
Marcar uma reunião depois do período menstrual. Evitar viagens na semana em que a cólica costuma chegar. Deixar o remédio na bolsa, na gaveta do trabalho e na mesa de cabeceira. Muitas mulheres organizam a vida em torno da menstruação tão naturalmente que deixam de perceber o tamanho da adaptação. É esse prejuízo, e não só a intensidade da dor, que merece atenção.

É precisamente este impacto no dia a dia, e não apenas a intensidade da dor medida numa escala, que merece investigação médica. Sentir dor pélvica incapacitante não é normal. A normalização social da dor menstrual atrasa o diagnóstico da endometriose: uma doença inflamatória crônica que afeta cerca de 10% das mulheres em idade fértil no mundo.

“Sentir dor não é normal e a cirurgia pode ser o melhor momento de fazer certo. Compreendemos que a dor importa e precisa ser ouvida” , diz Tiago Castilho, cirurgião oncológico com atuação em cirurgia ginecológica e cirurgia de endometriose profunda.

O custo invisível no trabalho: presenteísmo

Um dos estudos epidemiológicos mais relevantes sobre o impacto da doença (Fertility and Sterility) acompanhou 1.418 mulheres em 10 países e revelou que a endometriose causa uma perda média de 10,8 horas de trabalho por semana .

Surpreendentemente, a maior fatia desta perda não resulta de faltas ao trabalho (absenteísmo), mas sim do presenteísmo : a mulher está fisicamente presente no seu posto de trabalho, mas a cumprir tarefas sob dor intensa, com a sua concentração, energia e produtividade drasticamente reduzidas.

A necessidade de procurar avaliação médica surge quando a dor começa a interferir com os seguintes aspetos:

Atividades diárias: Precisar de medicação contínua para conseguir cuidar dos filhos ou cumprir compromissos.

Vida social e relacionamentos: Evitar a intimidade sexual, cancelar compromissos sociais ou isolar-se por exaustão física e emocional.

Carreira e estudos: Faltar a aulas, adiar prazos ou trabalhar sob sofrimento.

Se a menstruação dita o que pode ou não fazer no seu mês, não espere que a dor piore para procurar ajuda especializada.

O diagnóstico começa numa consulta detalhada sobre o histórico da dor e as suas limitações, seguida de exame clínico e exames de imagem específicos (como ultrassom com preparo intestinal ou ressonância magnética). Para pacientes que residem fora de Maringá, a avaliação inicial pode ser realizada por telemedicina.

A primeira consulta, segundo Tiago Castilho, serve para analisar os exames e discutir sintomas e preocupações. Quem mora fora de Maringá pode começar o atendimento online, mas a cirurgia, quando indicada, exige presença física. Para saber como funciona, veja a página de atendimento .

Quando a dor começa a determinar compromissos, trabalho, relações familiares e atividades cotidianas, ela merece ser investigada.

Há mais de 10 anos, Tiago Castilho atende e opera mulheres com endometriose e atua especialmente na avaliação de casos que podem exigir tratamento cirúrgico especializado. Sua experiência inclui videolaparoscopia e cirurgia robótica, com técnicas minimamente invasivas, e uma jornada de preparação e recuperação estruturada pelo Cuidado 360º.

Para mais informações ou agendamento de consulta, entre em contato pelo telefone (44) 99169-8161.

Tiago Castilho é Cirurgião Oncológico com atuação em Cirurgia Ginecológica e Cirurgia de Endometriose Profunda, mestre e doutor na área, com mais de 10 anos de experiência no tratamento cirúrgico da doença. CRM-PR 22590 | RQE 2911 | RQE 844.

articles.title: Mega-Sena concurso 3088: 18 apostas do Piauí acertam a quadra | G1
articles.standfirst: O prêmio para as apostas que acertassem as seis dezenas era de R$ 37,7 milhões. No entanto, ninguém levou a faixa principal e o valor acumulou para R$ 45 milhões.
articles.summary: O prêmio para as apostas que acertassem as seis dezenas era de R$ 37,7 milhões. No entanto, ninguém levou a faixa principal e o valor acumulou para R$ 45 milhões.
articles.body:
Dezoito apostas feitas no Piauí acertaram a quadra do concurso 3.088 da Mega-Sena, sorteado na noite de quinta-feira (18), em São Paulo. Cada bilhete premiado vai receber R$ 593,15. As apostas vencedoras foram registradas em sete municípios piauienses.

As dezenas sorteadas no concurso 3.088 foram: 10 - 21 - 24 - 28 - 34 - 44

As apostas premiadas foram registradas em Angical do Piauí , Floriano, Luís Correia , Picos , Piripiri , Regeneração e na capital Teresina .

Teresina teve o maior número de apostas premiadas, com oito bilhetes vencedores.

Confira a quantidade de apostas premiadas por município:

O prêmio para as apostas que acertassem as seis dezenas era de R$ 37,7 milhões. No entanto, ninguém levou a faixa principal e o valor acumulou para R$ 45 milhões.

A aposta simples da Mega-Sena, com seis dezenas, custa R$ 6. Os jogos podem ser registrados até as 20h (horário de Brasília) em casas lotéricas de todo o país ou pelos canais digitais da Caixa, no site e no aplicativo Loterias Caixa.

Os bolões digitais podem ser adquiridos até as 20h30 pelo portal Loterias Online e pelo aplicativo da Caixa.

Nas apostas pela internet, o pagamento pode ser feito por Pix, cartão de crédito ou internet banking, no caso de correntistas da Caixa Econômica Federal. Para jogar, é preciso ter 18 anos ou mais.

A Mega-Sena realiza três sorteios por semana: às terças-feiras, quintas-feiras e aos domingos.

Quais são as chances de ganhar na Mega-Sena?

As chances de ganhar variam conforme a quantidade de números escolhidos na aposta.

Em uma aposta simples, com seis números e custo de R$ 6, a probabilidade de acertar as seis dezenas é de uma em 50.063.860.

Já uma aposta com 20 dezenas, que custa R$ 232.560, tem probabilidade de uma em 1.292 de acertar os seis números e ganhar o prêmio principal, segundo a Caixa.

articles.title: BH instala câmeras para flagrar caminhões na faixa esquerda do Anel | G1
articles.standfirst: Equipamentos ainda estão em fase de implementação e não há data para início da operação. Infração pode render quatro pontos na CNH e multa de R$ 130,16.
articles.summary: Equipamentos ainda estão em fase de implementação e não há data para início da operação. Infração pode render quatro pontos na CNH e multa de R$ 130,16.
articles.body:
Câmera instalada no Anel Rodoviário de BH para fiscalizar veículos pesados que trafegam pela faixa da esquerda. — Foto: TV Globo

A Prefeitura de Belo Horizonte começou a instalar câmeras no Anel Rodoviário para fiscalizar veículos de grande porte que trafegam pela faixa da esquerda em trechos onde essa circulação é proibida. Os equipamentos ainda estão em fase de implementação, e a administração municipal não informou quando o sistema começará a operar.

As câmeras estão sendo instaladas no canteiro central da via e contam com flashes, o que permite registrar a passagem dos veículos também durante a noite. O sistema será usado para identificar motoristas que desrespeitam a sinalização.

Nos trechos onde há essa determinação, carretas, caminhões e outros veículos pesados devem trafegar pela faixa da direita. Segundo a prefeitura, quem descumprir a regra pode receber quatro pontos na Carteira Nacional de Habilitação (CNH) e multa de R$ 130,16.

Desde que a prefeitura assumiu a administração do Anel, a Guarda Municipal registrou 130 autuações por circulação de veículos de grande porte fora da faixa da direita. Os registros foram feitos entre junho de 2025 e outubro deste ano.

Para o especialista em segurança viária Frederico Rodrigues, a fiscalização eletrônica pode contribuir para aumentar o respeito à regra, mas não deve ser considerada a única medida necessária para tornar a via mais segura.

“Quando pesa no bolso, a atenção é um pouco maior. Ou seja, esse elemento vem a contribuir para a segurança viária, mas de forma alguma é a única solução”, afirmou.

A restrição também está relacionada à segurança no trânsito. Caminhões e ônibus têm pontos cegos e precisam de mais espaço para realizar determinadas manobras e frenagens. A presença desses veículos na faixa da esquerda pode aumentar os riscos para os demais usuários da via, especialmente durante ultrapassagens.

articles.title: Dívidas viraram uma bola de neve? Entenda os riscos da inadimplência | G1
articles.standfirst: No g1 Explica, a repórter Renata Ribeiro explica e simplifica os temas que dominam o noticiário econômico e mexem diretamente com o nosso bolso.
articles.summary: No g1 Explica, a repórter Renata Ribeiro explica e simplifica os temas que dominam o noticiário econômico e mexem diretamente com o nosso bolso.
articles.body:
Ter dívidas faz parte da vida financeira da maioria das pessoas. O problema começa quando elas deixam de ser pagas e viram inadimplência — sinal de que a dívida cresceu além da capacidade de pagamento, seja por juros altos, prazos curtos, imprevistos ou queda de renda.

Esse desequilíbrio já afeta mais do que as famílias. Com muitos atrasos, a inadimplência tende a encarecer o crédito, desacelerar a economia e dificultar contratações.

Sair desse ciclo exige estratégia, como priorizar dívidas caras, renegociar e evitar novos compromissos.

Neste vídeo, você vai entender os riscos da inadimplência e como escapar da bola de neve. Toda semana, o g1 Explica simplifica a economia, o mercado financeiro e a educação financeira, mostrando como tudo isso afeta o seu bolso.

articles.title: Irmãos são levados à força de festa e encontrados mortos em Cariacica | G1
articles.standfirst: Corpos tinham marcas de tiros na cabeça. Ainda não há confirmação se os irmãos foram mortos no local onde os corpos foram encontrados ou se foram levados até lá depois do crime.
articles.summary: Corpos tinham marcas de tiros na cabeça. Ainda não há confirmação se os irmãos foram mortos no local onde os corpos foram encontrados ou se foram levados até lá depois do crime.
articles.body:
Dois irmãos, de 18 e 19 anos, foram encontrados mortos na noite de quinta-feira (19), no bairro Vila Prudêncio, em Cariacica , na Grande Vitória. Os corpos de Paulo Rossi do Carmo, de 19 anos, e André Rossi do Carmo, de 18, estavam com as mãos amarradas para trás e marcas de tiros na cabeça.

Segundo informações preliminares da polícia, os jovens participavam de uma festa no bairro Santo Antônio, também em Cariacica, quando homens encapuzados chegaram ao local e retiraram os dois irmãos à força.

Em seguida, os suspeitos levaram os jovens para outra região, onde eles teriam sido assassinados. Os corpos foram encontrados em uma área conhecida como Rua da Matinha, em Vila Prudêncio, pouco depois das 22h.

Irmãos são levados à força de festa e encontrados mortos com mãos amarradas em Cariacica — Foto: Redes Sociais

Ainda não há confirmação se os irmãos foram mortos no local onde os corpos foram encontrados ou se foram levados até lá depois do crime.

De acordo com a polícia, os dois tinham passagens por envolvimento com o tráfico de drogas e por outros crimes. Essa possível ligação é uma das linhas consideradas na investigação sobre a motivação dos assassinatos.

O caso segue sob investigação. Até a última atualização desta reportagem, não hvia informações sobre suspeitos presos.

articles.title: Refugiados rohingyas: Turquia receberá 10 mil após decisão da CIJ | G1
articles.standfirst: Malásia anunciou acordo para enviar refugiados à Turquia; decisão internacional considerou genocídio assassinatos e violência sexual cometidos por forças de Mianmar em 2017.
articles.summary: Após a Corte Internacional de Justiça reconhecer o genocídio em Mianmar, a Turquia receberá 10 mil refugiados rohingyas em um programa de capacitação profissional.
articles.body:
Refugiados rohingya participam de um comício com o discurso do presidente da Assembleia Geral das Nações Unidas, Khalilur Rahman, após o veredicto da Corte Internacional de Justiça de que Mianmar cometeu genocídio contra os rohingya , em um campo de refugiados em Cox's Bazar, Bangladesh. — Foto: Mohammad Ponir Hossain/Reuters

A Malásia informou nesta sexta-feira (20) que reassentará 10 mil refugiados rohingyas na Turquia por meio de um programa estruturado de capacitação profissional, em uma iniciativa que seria uma das maiores envolvendo o reassentamento de rohingyas desde a repressão militar no estado de Rakhine, terra natal desse povo, em 2017.

O plano, anunciado pelo vice-primeiro-ministro da Malásia, Ahmad Zahid Hamidi, foi divulgado um dia depois de a Corte Internacional de Justiça decidir que os assassinatos e a violência sexual generalizada cometidos pelas forças de segurança de Mianmar contra o povo rohingya em 2017 configuraram genocídio patrocinado pelo Estado .

A proposta faz parte dos esforços do governo para lidar com a situação dos refugiados rohingyas na Malásia de forma mais "coordenada, eficaz e humana", afirmou Ahmad Zahid em comunicado.

"Saúdo o acordo do governo da Turquia para receber 10 mil refugiados rohingyas. Isso representa um passo importante nos esforços da Malásia para encontrar uma solução de longo prazo para uma questão que há muito tempo impõe desafios à gestão da migração e à segurança nacional", afirmou.

Ahmad Zahid disse que a iniciativa com a Turquia poderá servir de modelo de como países podem trabalhar em conjunto para administrar o reassentamento de refugiados.

"O governo trabalhará com as autoridades turcas, o Acnur e as agências pertinentes para coordenar a seleção dos participantes, o treinamento, a documentação e o reassentamento. A implementação levará em consideração as necessidades do mercado de trabalho, o consentimento das pessoas envolvidas e as normas internacionais aplicáveis", afirmou.

O Ministério das Relações Exteriores da Turquia não respondeu imediatamente a um pedido de comentário.

A Malásia tem sofrido pressão para enviar refugiados rohingyas de volta a Mianmar em meio ao aumento das tensões com as comunidades locais. Segundo o Acnur, a Malásia tinha cerca de 193 mil refugiados registrados de Mianmar no fim de fevereiro, aproximadamente dois terços deles rohingyas.

A Malásia enviou mais de 10 mil cidadãos de Mianmar de volta ao país desde janeiro.

articles.title: Como é a experiência da cirurgia de endometriose com robô? | G1
articles.standfirst: Console, imagem em 3D e instrumentos articulados: estudos com 2.021 pacientes mostram que a via robótica tem segurança semelhante à tradicional.
articles.summary: Console, imagem em 3D e instrumentos articulados: estudos com 2.021 pacientes mostram que a via robótica tem segurança semelhante à tradicional.
articles.body:
Na cirurgia robótica, é sempre o cirurgião quem comanda cada detalhe. Sentado em um console na sala de operação, ele enxerga a pelve em uma tela tridimensional ampliada e guia instrumentos articulados por pequenos cortes na barriga. O robô reproduz os movimentos das mãos do médico com máxima precisão, mas não toma nenhuma decisão sozinho.

Quem precisa operar a endometriose provavelmente já ouviu falar da cirurgia robótica e da videolaparoscopia. Com isso, vem a dúvida natural: qual é a melhor opção?

A resposta começa por entender que a videolaparoscopia tradicional continua sendo uma técnica excelente e super consolidada. O diferencial do robô está no refinamento da ferramenta, que traz ainda mais precisão para o cirurgião.

"A tecnologia robótica eleva o padrão de precisão que oferecemos às pacientes. Representa a integração entre a experiência cirúrgica humana e a tecnologia de ponta" , destaca, Tiago Castilho, cirurgião oncológico com atuação em cirurgia ginecológica e cirurgia de endometriose profunda, que opera com os dois métodos.

O que a tecnologia muda na sala de cirurgia

Os instrumentos robóticos possuem articulações que reproduzem os movimentos do punho humano e dispõem de filtros que eliminam microtremores.

A visão tridimensional em alta definição facilita a dissecação em espaços reduzidos e em áreas onde a doença se encontra aderida a estruturas nobres, como o intestino, a bexiga ou os ureteres.

O planeamento cirúrgico precede a tecnologia

Independentemente da ferramenta escolhida, o sucesso da intervenção depende da qualificação da equipa e do planeamento pré e pós-operatório. As diretrizes da Sociedade Europeia de Reprodução Humana e Embriologia (ESHRE 2022) recomendam que casos de endometriose profunda sejam operados em centros de referência, pois fazer uma boa primeira cirurgia é o passo mais importante para garantir o alívio da dor e evitar que a doença volte.

De acordo com Castilho, a escolha entre o robô e a videolaparoscopia depende de exames de imagem bem detalhados, do tamanho da doença e das necessidades de cada mulher.

Seja qual for a técnica, a operação é só uma etapa. Para entender o que vem depois, veja o artigo A cirurgia é só o começo: o que ninguém te conta sobre a verdadeira recuperação da endometriose .

A escolha da tecnologia deve acompanhar as necessidades de cada cirurgia, e não o contrário.

Há mais de 10 anos operando mulheres com endometriose, Tiago Castilho tem experiência e formação em cirurgia minimamente invasiva, incluindo videolaparoscopia e cirurgia robótica.

Para mais informações ou agendamento de consulta, entre em contato pelo telefone (44) 99169-8161.

Tiago Castilho é Cirurgião Oncológico com atuação em Cirurgia Ginecológica e Cirurgia de Endometriose Profunda, mestre e doutor na área, com mais de 10 anos de experiência no tratamento cirúrgico da doença. CRM-PR 22590 | RQE 2911 | RQE 844.

articles.title: Mulher negra se torna a primeira líder trans em multinacional de SP | G1
articles.standfirst: Em dois anos, Darllene Martins, de 31 anos, saiu de um contrato temporário de 10 dias na função de auxiliar para comandar 20 profissionais de logística na empresa em Lençóis Paulista (SP).
articles.summary: Aos 31 anos, Darllene Martins superou barreiras para se tornar a primeira mulher trans negra em cargo de liderança na logística de uma multinacional em SP.
articles.body:
Trocar a segurança de um emprego fixo por um contrato temporário de apenas dez dias parecia uma aposta arriscada. Para Darllene Martins, de 31 anos, foi a porta de entrada para fazer história.

De auxiliar de expedição no carregamento, em dois anos ela construiu caminho dentro de uma multinacional de celulose em Lençóis Paulista (SP) até assumir o comando de uma equipe de cerca de 20 profissionais no setor de logística, tornando-se a primeira mulher trans negra a ocupar um cargo de liderança na companhia.

Mulher negra se torna a primeira líder trans em multinacional do interior de SP — Foto: Bracell/Reprodução

Nesta sexta-feira (20), celebra-se o Dia da Consciência Negra, data dedicada à reflexão sobre o combate ao racismo, às desigualdades estruturais e à valorização da população negra no Brasil, como é o caso da história de Darllene.

Darllene Martins é a primeira mulher trans a ocupar um cargo de liderança em empresa de produção de celulose em Lençóis Paulista (SP) — Foto: Bracell/Reprodução

Em entrevista ao g1 , Darllene contou que assumir o cargo exige jogo de cintura diário diante das barreiras ainda impostas no mercado de trabalho.

“Ser uma mulher trans e preta à frente de uma equipe é desafiador. A gente ainda vive numa sociedade machista, e isso pesa quando uma mulher ocupa um cargo de liderança”, afirma.

Apesar do receio quando chegou à indústria, ela conta que recebeu apoio desde os primeiros dias e transformou a própria conquista em incentivo para outras profissionais.

“Hoje, à frente de uma equipe de auxiliares na logística, quero puxar outras mulheres comigo. Quero que elas também se vejam em condições de assumir uma liderança e tenham oportunidades para chegar lá”, ressalta.

Do primeiro emprego aos 13 anos à liderança

Antes de entrar na empresa de celulose, Darllene passou por diferentes áreas. Começou a trabalhar aos 13 anos como garçonete no buffet da tia, foi recepcionista na Casa de Cultura de Lençóis Paulista, atuou com telemarketing e ficou seis anos no atendimento de uma padaria.

“Também trabalhei numa fábrica de cadeiras, embalando produtos. O atendimento me ensinou muito sobre como conversar com pessoas diferentes, e isso me ajuda até hoje na liderança”, revela.

Foi justamente uma colega da fábrica de cadeiras que avisou sobre a vaga na produtora de celulose e despertou o interesse dela pela área.

“Eu queria conhecer a área de logística e decidi trocar um emprego fixo por um contrato de dez dias como auxiliar de expedição, no carregamento. O contrato foi prorrogado por um mês e, depois, fui efetivada”, relembra.

Depois da efetivação, voltou a estudar e cresceu internamente até assumir a liderança operacional.

“Na empresa, fui conhecendo a operação e assumindo novas responsabilidades. Uma das primeiras oportunidades foi liderar uma equipe pequena. Também recebi incentivo para voltar a estudar e comecei a cursar Gestão de Recursos Humanos. Quando surgiu a vaga de líder de logística, participei do processo seletivo interno e conquistei a posição. Hoje, sou líder operacional de uma equipe de cerca de 20 auxiliares”, acrescenta.

Darlene trabalhou em diversos lugares antes de chegar em cargo de liderança em empresa de Lençóis Paulista (SP) — Foto: Bracell/Reprodução

Ao longo da carreira, Darllene enfrentou situações de desrespeito, mas afirma que prefere responder com conversa e informação.

“Quando isso acontece, procuro lidar com diálogo. Sempre tive jogo de cintura para conversar e mostrar por que certas ideias sobre pessoas trans são preconceituosas”, pontua.

Para ela, ocupar esse espaço vai além da realização pessoal e serve de referência para que outras mulheres trans busquem crescimento profissional.

“Quero que outras mulheres trans também cheguem onde eu cheguei”, destaca. “Eu quero que outras mulheres trans olhem para a minha história e pensem: ‘Se a Darllene conseguiu, eu também posso conseguir’”, deseja.

“Se eu pudesse resumir essa conquista em uma palavra, seria possibilidade. É isso que eu quero que elas vejam na minha história: a possibilidade de construir a própria carreira e chegar a lugares que talvez ainda nem tenham se imaginado ocupando”, finaliza.

articles.title: Qualcomm lays off hundreds in California; as CEO Cristiano Amon says: We must have the right people in the right ...
articles.summary: Qualcomm is cutting hundreds of jobs in California as part of a broader global workforce reduction.
articles.body: Qualcomm is cutting hundreds of jobs in California as part of a broader global workforce reduction. Company CEO Cristiano Amon has reportedly framed the move as a “performance-focused” overhaul of the company's talent. Citing state notices filed in California this week, The New York Post reports Qualcomm is permanently laying off 517 employees across two key hubs: San Diego, where 442 positions are being eliminated at the company's headquarters, and Santa Clara County where the remaining 75 job cuts will take place across its facilities.While Qualcomm employed roughly 52,000 people worldwide as of September 2025, the full scale of the cuts outside California remains unclear. The job cuts will be effective January 12, 2027.Why Qualcomm is cutting jobs nowIn an internal memo previously viewed by news agency Reuters, Amon explained to staff that the layoffs followed annual employee reviews and were aimed at addressing areas where the business “has consistently fallen short of expectations.” He noted that decisions were guided by business priorities, organisational needs and the specific skills and expertise required moving forward.“As we have expanded the business, so have the competencies ⁠and skills we require. We must have the right people in the right roles so they can perform at their best and the company can continue to succeed,” Amon wrote in the memo.Pivoting from smartphones to AI data centersQualcomm’s push to reshape its workforce comes as the company works to pivot beyond its traditional stronghold, manufacturing semiconductors for mobile phones and wireless technology, toward the power-hungry data centers fueling the artificial intelligence (AI) boom.Through this expansion, Qualcomm is aiming to capture AI chip market share from rival Nvidia. The shift is also driven by financial necessity. During its latest earnings report in late July, Qualcomm warned that revenue tied to Apple products is expected to decline faster than previously anticipated, noting that it hopes growth in the data center market will make up for that lost revenue by fiscal year 2027.Fearless legend or grounded realist? articles.title: Lula visits ailing Chief Raoni as Brazil recognises Indigenous land
articles.summary: Lula honours Raoni in Mato Grosso, celebrating his legacy and advancing protection for Kayapo and Yudja ancestral lands.
articles.body:
Brazilian President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva has visited the ailing Indigenous leader Raoni Metuktire, a lifelong defender of the Amazon rainforest, as the country’s government recognised the chief’s ancestral land as Indigenous territory.

Lula met the 94-year-old chief on Thursday in Peixoto de Azevedo, a city in Mato Grosso state, near the Amazonian village where Raoni has lived for decades.

Raoni, who is known for his wooden lip plate, is receiving palliative care for gastrointestinal cancer and was hospitalised for a few days last week with a lung infection and low blood pressure.

“There is no Brazilian more authentic than our comrade Raoni,” Lula said. “He represents the past, he represents the present, and his ideas represent the future of Indigenous peoples in this country.”

At a ceremony later, Brazil’s Justice Ministry declared the Kapot Nhinore Indigenous Territory to be in the permanent possession of the Mebengokre, also known as Kayapo, and Yudja peoples. It is a crucial step towards formal demarcation of the land by presidential decree. Raoni has campaigned for its protection for three decades.

Lula said he was “deeply distressed” to hear of Raoni’s hospitalisation while he was at the COP31 climate summit in Turkiye. “I wanted to resolve the issue regarding the land where Raoni was born while he was still alive,” he said.

Raoni’s grandson, Roiti Metuktire, told the AFP news agency the decision had come as a surprise to the family. “It’s his last wish,” he said.

Raoni left his home in the Amazon in the late 1980s to travel the world, meeting presidents, popes and royals to warn about the destruction of the planet’s biggest rainforest. He walked beside Lula at his inauguration in 2023 .

Experts see demarcated Indigenous territories as one of the best barriers against deforestation, as the Amazon moves closer to a tipping point at which it could become a drier, savannah-like ecosystem.

The territory covers about 362,000 hectares (nearly 900,000 acres). Eloy Terena, Brazil’s minister of Indigenous peoples, said it is 84 percent forest.

A 2023 Greenpeace report said more than 47,000 hectares (116,000 acres) were used for pasture or soy.

Rural producers have campaigned against the demarcation, saying it would have severe economic consequences for thousands of non-Indigenous people who live and farm there.

“There is still a bit of a battle ahead. There are over two hundred properties on this land,” Lula said.

Brazil has almost 800 Indigenous lands, about 60 percent of them fully regularised. Lula resumed demarcations after returning to office in 2023, with 20 territories fully demarcated in three years. They remain under pressure from agribusiness, illegal gold mining and logging.

This week, about 20 emaciated members of an isolated Indigenous group emerged from the forest in another part of the Amazon to ask for food, highlighting the challenges faced by Indigenous communities nationwide.

articles.title: A French woman bought a black ceramic lamp for €20 at a flea market; it was later identified as a rare work by French ceramicist Georges Jouve and has now sold for €251,000 at a Paris auction, setting a world record for one of his lamps
articles.summary: A black ceramic lamp sat on a stall at a brocante in northern France, one object among hundreds that shoppers passed on their way to something else.
articles.body: A black ceramic lamp sat on a stall at a brocante in northern France, one object among hundreds that shoppers passed on their way to something else. Then a woman stopped. Her eyes twinkled, and she reached for it. She thought the lamp was a steal at €20. She bought it and took it home. Later, her daughter noticed something engraved on it. A call to an auction house in Paris revealed that it was worth a fortune. The lamp turned out to be by designer Georges Jouve and has now sold at auction for €251,000, about 12,000 times what the French woman originally paid for it at the flea market, according to a report by The Connexion. The woman who bought it has not been publicly named, and the family has kept a low profile since the sale.The black ceramic lamp from a flea marketSometimes, it takes the right person to recognise the value of an ordinary-looking object. Many shoppers at the brocante passed by the black lamp. None of them thought it was a rare find until this French woman came along. Her eyes lit up at the sight of the black ceramic lamp. It was unlike anything she had seen before. The lamp's distinctive shape and glossy finish caught her eye. Something about it seemed special. She asked the seller how much it cost. The asking price? Just €20. She didn’t bargain; she paid the price and took it home. After a while, the woman moved the lamp to a cupboard. It spent months there before anyone looked at it properly. When the woman’s daughter began clearing out the house, she noticed the lamp. She found it appealing. While inspecting it, she turned the piece over and found a signature engraved on its base: Jouve.The daughter did what most people would do first. She searched for the name. That led her to NEO Enchères, a Paris auction house that already knew Jouve’s work and had sold a lamp of the same model before. The family got in touch and made the trip to Paris with the piece in hand.The experts’ verdict was good news on two counts. The lamp was authentic, and it was in very good condition. Condition matters more with ceramics than many owners expect. Glaze can craze and bodies can chip over the decades, and every flaw takes value with it. But this one was in pristine condition.The auction house estimated the lamp at between €80,000 and €120,000 ahead of its sale on 29 October. There were around ten potential buyers, some bidding in the room and about six on the telephone, the auction house said. The contest narrowed to two European buyers, who kept raising each other’s bids until one stopped. With buyer’s fees included, the final price reached €251,000. That is more than 12,000 times what the woman paid. The auction house says it is a world auction record for a lamp by Jouve. “We always hope to achieve records, but we weren't expecting such a high price,” Quentin Charraudeau, president of NEO Enchères, told the outlet. “It's something exceptional.”The auction price is explained by how rare the piece is. “We don't know exactly how many lamps of this model Georges Jouve produced, but what is certain is that it is rare. We don't see it very often,” Charraudeau told the outlet.Born in 1910, Georges Jouve made sculptural ceramics for modernist interiors, working first in Paris and later in Aix-en-Provence. His pieces are now collected by people who know his name. Most of the lamps in auction catalogues carry his signature, but not all of them are worth a second look, which is what makes this find unusual. He died in 1964, at the age of 54.Talking about the success of the sale, Charraudeau added, “We knew we had an object that our collectors were looking for. I was very excited because I knew several collectors would compete for it, and that is exactly what happened.”You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Gaza Civil Defence struggles to rescue lives as vehicles break down
articles.summary: More than 85 percent of Gaza Civil Defence vehicles are out of service as crews struggle to reach trapped people.
articles.body:
Gaza City, Gaza Strip – Palestinian Civil Defence crews heard an explosion nearby and rushed to respond. But instead of taking a fire engine – the only vehicle available to the team at the time – they had to grab their equipment and rush to help on foot. The fire engine wasn’t working.

“We heard the strike, opened the vehicle, took our equipment and ran,” said Abdullah al-Majdalawi, a Civil Defence field officer, describing the response to an Israeli attack near the al-Qattan Centre on November 3. It took about 10 minutes for the crew to reach the site, carrying their equipment, and then carrying injured people back. They also recovered the body of someone killed in the strike.

It was another example of how the breakdown of emergency vehicles is affecting rescue teams’ ability to reach people quickly.

In a separate incident in southern Gaza City’s Sabra neighbourhood last month, the vehicle the Civil Defence team was using broke down while the crew was responding to an Israeli air strike on the area.

By the time they were able to reach the scene, several people had been killed, and others were critically injured. Al-Majdalawi believes that arriving sooner could have given some of the injured a better chance of survival.

During another mission, in 2024, the crew had to rely on a man with a donkey-drawn cart to transport them and their equipment.

“People were astonished to see Civil Defence personnel travelling that way… but this is what we can do,” al-Majdalawi said.

The only dedicated rescue vehicle in Gaza governorate, a Toyota Hilux pick-up truck, has been out of service for weeks. It is more than 20 years old, according to al-Majdalawi, and has been worn down by years of use and the intense workload during Israel’s genocidal war, which began in October 2023.

The crew has tried everything to keep it running, including patching its tyres with flour dough when proper repairs were not possible. The vehicle needs a power steering pump, tyres and other parts. Its turbo system is also faulty, while problems with its lights make night-time missions more dangerous.

“We have exhausted every means and every method to keep this vehicle running,” al-Majdalawi said.

Without it, crews have to rely on larger fire engines for rescue operations. These are harder to manoeuvre through streets crowded with tents, makeshift shelters, and market stalls.

If emergencies happen simultaneously in different areas, and there aren’t enough vehicles available, teams have to choose where to respond first.

The situation reflects a wider collapse in the capacity of Gaza’s Civil Defence.

Emergency teams are still responding to strikes, fires, and building collapses, but their ability to reach people is increasingly constrained by a lack of functioning vehicles and equipment.

The United Nations Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA) warned in a May 1 report that restrictions on the entry of engine oil and spare parts for vehicles and rubble-removal machinery were having an increasingly severe impact on humanitarian operations in Gaza.

It said prolonged shortages were causing vehicles and generators to break down beyond repair, affecting the movement of humanitarian teams, ambulance services, and other essential operations.

Raed al-Dahshan, director of Gaza City’s Civil Defence, said more than 85 percent of the department’s vehicles were out of operation, leaving only about 15 percent working across the territory.

Many vehicles have been in service since 1994, when the Palestinian Authority was established, and have carried out tens of thousands of missions. Years of use, damaged roads, and the demands of the war have left much of the fleet worn out.

Al-Dahshan said many Civil Defence vehicles have exceeded their expected service life and urgently need replacing. International fire-service guidelines generally recommend replacing front-line fire engines after 15 to 20 years of operation.

Repairing the vehicles has become increasingly difficult. Local workshops have limited capacity, and the department often has to refurbish old parts or find alternatives because replacement parts are unavailable.

At the department’s maintenance workshop, maintenance officer Abd al-Fattah al-Nimra works alongside a team trying to keep the ageing fleet operational.

With proper parts unavailable or prohibitively expensive, mechanics resort to temporary fixes and substitute components. These may get a vehicle moving again, but they cannot offer the reliability or performance of the original parts.

“Since the beginning of the war, we have faced many problems with spare parts and their high prices,” al-Nimra said. “The parts that run out are not replaced because the occupation prevents them from entering.”

He said the team tried to find temporary alternatives wherever possible, but they did not perform as well as original components. Even basic items such as tyres had become extremely expensive, while the cost and shortage of engine oil added another burden to already limited maintenance budgets.

Since the beginning of the war in October 2023, Israeli restrictions on the entry of essential supplies into Gaza, including vehicle spare parts and engine oil, have made it increasingly difficult for emergency services to maintain their fleets.

OCHA warned that shortages of these supplies were causing vehicles and generators to break down, in some cases beyond repair, while also affecting heavy machinery needed to remove rubble and keep essential services running.

The only rescue vehicle serving Gaza governorate needs a power steering pump, tyres, a turbo component and warning lights identifying it as a rescue vehicle, al-Nimra said. Although some parts can be found in the local market, their prices are beyond the department’s available budget.

The shortage of equipment comes as Civil Defence teams continue to respond to the consequences of Israel’s war on Gaza, including air strikes, fires, and buildings at risk of collapse.

With winter now under way, officials fear that heavy rain and strong winds will further weaken already damaged structures, creating more emergencies at a time when rescue teams have fewer vehicles and limited equipment to respond.

Those fears have already been borne out. Heavy rains in early November caused damaged buildings to collapse and flooded displacement sites across Gaza. But Civil Defence teams were only able to respond to a minority of the distress calls they received.

Most other callers were given guidance over the phone, highlighting the gap between the growing needs and the department’s capacity to respond.

More than 140 Civil Defence personnel have been killed during the war, al-Dahshan said.

The department has fewer than 1,000 employees across Gaza’s five governorates, and many continue working despite inadequate resources and a lack of regular salaries.

Civil Defence personnel and equipment are entitled to protection under international humanitarian law, including Article 62 of Additional Protocol I to the Geneva Conventions, which provides for the protection of civilian civil defence organisations and their personnel.

Al-Dahshan warned that without urgent support, the department could reach a point where it is unable to respond to people’s calls. The time it takes to reach an injured person can determine whether they survive, he said.

For al-Majdalawi, the immediate needs are basic: functioning vehicles, spare parts, tyres, engine oil and fuel.

“We are not asking for much,” he said. “We need tyres, engine oil and fuel. We are ready to dig through the rubble for hours and days to rescue people, but we need the equipment to do that.”

“If the world cannot stop the war on Gaza,” al-Dahshan said, “at the very least it should enable humanitarian services to rescue the injured before they die.”

articles.title: Four friends paid £1.3 million for a derelict Welsh mansion built in 1776 and spent £700,000 restoring it; after facing prosecution over alleged unauthorised work, the local council dropped its case
articles.summary: A group of four friends who bought a neglected historic mansion in mid-Wales for £1.3 million have won a lengthy dispute with the local council over
articles.body: A group of four friends who bought a neglected historic mansion in mid-Wales for £1.3 million have won a lengthy dispute with the local council over renovation work carried out on the property. The owners of Llanerchydol Hall, who invested a further £700,000 in bringing the estate back to life, had faced the prospect of prosecution over alleged unauthorised alterations. However, Powys County Council has now dropped its case, bringing a halt to the planning enforcement battle. The property and its restoration journey came into the spotlight through Channel 4’s television series Help! We Bought a Hotel!, which followed the friends as they attempted to transform the deteriorating mansion into a hospitality business.The four owners are Benjamin Sutterby, George Dodge, Richard Stokes and Ranjeet Kaur Saini. Their ambitious purchase involved taking on a substantial restoration project, with the aim of turning the historic building and its grounds into a destination for visitors. The dispute centred on building regulations and the permissions required for work on a protected historic property. The owners were accused of failing to submit full plans for building control approval, notify the council before starting construction and apply to regularise work that had already been completed. If found guilty, they could have faced unlimited fines.The matter had previously escalated after Powys County Council refused retrospective planning permission for some of the proposed work in June 2023. Despite the refusal, renovation activity continued, prompting the authority to issue a temporary stop notice. The heritage body Cadw also received complaints from members of the public about work taking place at the site.The prosecution was due to be heard before a district judge earlier in November. However, council prosecutors withdrew the case shortly before the scheduled trial. A Powys County Council spokesperson confirmed that the authority had informed the court it was withdrawing its prosecution against Llanerchydol Hall and others and had requested that the trial be vacated. The decision brings the criminal proceedings to an end, although it does not, by itself, establish that all the renovation work has received planning or building-control approval.The scale of the undertaking becomes clearer when looking at the mansion’s history. Built in 1776 by wealthy tea trader David Pugh, Llanerchydol Hall occupies a picturesque setting outside Welshpool. The original house was constructed on the site of an earlier building believed to have been destroyed by fire. It remained in the Pugh family for 136 years and underwent several alterations over the decades.The property is recognised for its historic architecture and landscaped surroundings. Its parkland and gardens include a Japanese garden dating to the 1920s, ornamental planting, mature trees and historic features that contribute to the estate’s heritage significance. The hall itself is Grade II* listed, placing it among Wales’s particularly important historic buildings.The friends have been trying to make the restoration financially sustainable by opening completed rooms in the west wing for paying guests and using the income to fund further work on the neglected east wing. They have also explored converting the property’s stables into additional accommodation. The financial demands extend beyond construction, with annual building insurance reported to exceed £20,000.Their appearance on Help! We Bought a Hotel! brought viewers inside the challenges of reviving the sprawling property, from its deteriorating interiors to the practical and financial difficulties of running a historic estate. With the prosecution now withdrawn, the owners have cleared a significant hurdle in their effort to revive Llanerchydol Hall. articles.title: Tears of joy, prayers for return home: Rohingya react to genocide ruling
articles.summary: For refugees, the ICJ ruling that Myanmar committed genocide is a vindication. But will they be able to return home?
articles.body:
Dhaka, Bangladesh — Umme Ruman was watching the news on her mobile phone from her shelter in Camp 1E of the Rohingya refugee camps in Cox’s Bazar, Bangladesh. She had been waiting for the International Court of Justice (ICJ) verdict since the afternoon. But poor internet connectivity kept interrupting the live broadcast.

Then she opened Facebook and saw a headline: “ICJ confirms Myanmar committed genocide.”

Overwhelmed, she jumped. Her sister-in-law was cooking. Ruman rushed to hug her. Before she could explain what had happened, she broke down in tears.

“I celebrated with tears of joy because, for the first time, the world acknowledged what happened to us,” she said.

On Thursday, the ICJ found Myanmar responsible for genocide against the Rohingya during brutal military operations in 2017, in which the court found more than 10,000 people had been killed.

The landmark judgement in the case, brought before the court by The Gambia, recognised the atrocities committed against the community after years of denial. For refugees who have spent nearly a decade waiting for justice, the ruling brought a wave of relief, emotion and renewed hope.

“For me, this is not simply a legal verdict. It is proof of our suffering,” Ruman said.

Across the camps, people followed the announcement on mobile phones, laptops and large screens. Some watched with friends. Others gathered with their families. Many turned to Facebook and YouTube to follow the proceedings.

Eighteen-year-old Mohammad Rehan watched with his community teacher and friends on a laptop. “Some women were crying, while others were praying to Allah,” he said. “I did not do anything special. I just sat there and listened, hoping to hear some good news that would give us a peaceful life in the future.”

For Rehan, the first thought was that the verdict could potentially open the door for the Rohingya to return home. “Just imagining that made me so happy,” he said.

The news soon spread through the blocks. Rehan said people were celebrating, while elderly refugees discussed the case and The Gambia’s role in bringing it before the court. The small West African nation was not directly affected by the violence against the Rohingya. Still, it acted as a party to the 1948 Genocide Convention, under which all member states have an obligation to prevent and address genocide. In 2022, the court ruled that The Gambia had standing to bring the case.

Rehan’s mother was also delighted when he told her about the ruling. “She was saying that we had won and that we would be able to return to our homeland,” he said.

The celebrations came against a backdrop of difficult living conditions. Rain fell over the camps on Thursday as Cyclone Akvan bore down on the Bay of Bengal, adding to the discomfort of families living in cramped shelters.

It was a reminder that while the verdict had brought recognition to their suffering, it had not changed the daily realities of refugee life. Nurul Amin, a Rohingya youth, said he was happy when the court recognised the genocide, but the announcement also brought back painful memories.

“I was happy, but I was also remembering what happened to us in 2017. I was remembering the horrific military operation, the violence I experienced and the home I had to leave behind,” he said.

Rohingya activist Rohimullah said the announcement was difficult to put into words. It reminded him of those the community had lost and the darkest days of their displacement. He described the judgement as a moment of relief and renewed hope, but said it could not bring back loved ones or erase painful memories.

Nasir Uddin, a professor of anthropology at the University of Chittagong who researches the Rohingya crisis, said the ICJ ruling was important to ensure justice and accountability from the victims’ perspective.

“In the 21st century, we talk about liberal democracy, globalisation and global justice. Yet such a massive genocide happened before our eyes. The judgement was essential to establish the concept of global justice,” he said.

Michael Kugelman, a resident senior fellow for South Asia at the Atlantic Council, said the ruling meant that Dhaka would need stronger assurances from Myanmar about the safe return of Rohingya refugees under any repatriation arrangement.

“I think that this will also have some impact on the dynamics around negotiations between Bangladesh and Myanmar on the return of Rohingya refugees, now that an international court has said that they experienced genocide,” Kugelman told Al Jazeera.

For the Rohingya, however, the hope of going home remains central. They want accountability for those responsible for the atrocities, the restoration of their rights and citizenship, and a safe and dignified return to Myanmar.

Nurul Amin said he hoped the international community would look beyond the humanitarian crisis and address the political causes of their displacement. He said he wanted freedom in Myanmar, democracy and an end to discrimination and military dictatorship.

“We are hoping this judgement will lead to something more – that we will finally be able to return home with our rights and dignity,” he said.

Maung Solaiman Shah contributed to this story.

articles.title: Noida bride suffers burn injuries during laser hair removal therapy ahead of wedding, family fights 15-year legal battle, consumer commission orders clinic to refund Rs 99,000 with 6% interest and and Rs 55,000 in compensation and costs
articles.summary: NOIDA: A Noida woman who suffered burn injuries and blisters on her back and legs after undergoing laser hair removal treatment ahead of her marriage has
articles.body: NOIDA: A Noida woman who suffered burn injuries and blisters on her back and legs after undergoing laser hair removal treatment ahead of her marriage has won a 15-year legal battle against a hair and skin clinic. The District Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission has directed the clinic to refund Rs 99,000, with 6% annual interest, and pay Rs 50,000 in compensation and Rs 5,000 towards litigation costs.President Anil Kumar Pundir and member Anju Sharma, in an order dated Nov 4, held Berkowits Hair and Skin Clinic, Sector 18, Noida, and its proprietor Seema Goel guilty of deficiency in service. The clinic has been directed to make the payment within 30 days.The complaint was filed on Dec 12, 2013, by the woman through her mother, Santosh Redu, alleging deficiency in service and unfair trade practices.According to the complaint, the woman approached the clinic after seeing its advertisements, seeking permanent hair removal ahead of her marriage, scheduled for Sep 9, 2011. She was assured that the treatment would be completed in four to six months through six or seven sittings, under the supervision of doctors and experienced laser technicians. The total cost was Rs 99,000, which she paid in three instalments.She underwent her first session on Feb 2, 2011, and was told that results would become visible after two or three sittings. However, during her third session on May 22, she experienced severe burning sensations, pain and itching on her back and legs. She subsequently developed burn marks and blisters.When she reported the injuries, clinic staff allegedly advised her to apply skin creams. A dermatologist examined her on May 25 and prescribed medication for seven days.The woman told the commission that the injuries, allegedly caused by excessive exposure to laser rays, disrupted her marriage preparations and forced her to postpone the wedding. She also said she had to bear the cost of subsequent medical treatment.She later approached the chief medical officer (CMO), Noida, who examined her injuries and concluded that they were caused by overexposure to laser rays. Despite repeated calls and emails, the clinic allegedly refused to refund the treatment charges.Clinic denies negligenceIn its written reply, the clinic denied the allegations and argued that the complaint of medical negligence was not supported by an expert opinion from a competent doctor or medical board.It claimed that the woman had been attended to by Dr Shimpy Singh at its Noida branch on Jan 2, 2011, when potential complications, including skin irritation, itching and burns, were explained to her. She paid the first instalment of Rs 50,000 that day and signed an informed-consent form, the clinic said.The clinic added that details of the treatment and the body parts covered were recorded in her treatment history, which she signed. The remaining instalments were paid on March 27 and May 1, which, it claimed, indicated her satisfaction with the treatment.It further argued that the technician had repeatedly checked whether the laser intensity was bearable, but the woman believed higher intensity would produce better results and said she could tolerate it.The clinic claimed she was advised to apply an ointment called Fusibet and use ice on the affected areas in case of burns or irritation, but did not follow the instructions.Maintaining that the treatment was administered with due care and in accordance with medical standards, the clinic said no expert had established any lapse on its part. It also cited its 25 years of experience and claimed to have served more than three lakh customers through a panel of dermatologists and BHMS doctors.Commission finds clinic deficient in serviceAfter examining the documents and arguments, the commission observed that the clinic's own version showed that the third session was conducted by a laser technician. However, it had produced no evidence to establish that a qualified dermatologist was physically present and supervising the procedure throughout.The commission rejected the clinic's argument that the woman had repeatedly said she could tolerate the laser intensity, calling it self-serving and uncorroborated. It observed that even if she had made such statements, the clinic remained responsible for monitoring her condition during the procedure.The panel also noted that the technician continued the treatment despite her complaints, while the doctor examined her only after burn marks and blisters had developed."This conduct falls short of the standard of care expected of a clinic offering laser treatment and constitutes deficiency in service," the commission held.It also rejected the clinic's reliance on the informed-consent form, observing that consent to the known risks of a procedure did not absolve a clinic of responsibility for negligent treatment."A patient may consent to the inherent risk of a procedure, but not to injury caused by failure to monitor the procedure, excessive exposure, or continuation of treatment despite complaints of burning," the commission said.You Can Also Check: Gold Rate in Noida | Silver Rate in Noida | Bank Holidays in Noida | Public Holidays in Noida | Noida AQI | Weather in Noida | Petrol Price in Noida | Diesel Price in Noida | CNG Price in Noida | LPG Price in NoidaStay updated with the latest Noida news. articles.title: 'My frustrating 10-year-wait for arthritis diagnosis'
articles.summary: Clare Base lived with persistent pain before her Axial Spondyloarthritis diagnosis.
articles.body:
A woman said a decade-long wait to get diagnosed with a painful inflammatory arthritis left her frustrated and, at times, unable to walk.

Clare Base, who is in her 40s, from Portishead, said she lived with persistent pain which caused mobility issues and sleeplessness before she was diagnosed with ankylosing spondylitis, a form of axial spondyloarthritis (axSpA).

It comes as a new targeted awareness campaign for the condition, which affects one in 200 adults in the UK, is launched for health professionals across Bristol and Bath.

Base said she believed the campaign would make a difference and help ensure others struggling with sciatica and severe back pain are taken seriously.

Base said she started getting back pain, stiffness and sciatica in her 20s but her GP was unable to find a diagnosis.

"I thought at that age, I shouldn't be suffering in that way."

"Some days I could barely walk, barely put one foot in front of the other, if I ever sat down for too long, I would just feel the impact of it," said Base.

"My sleep was massively disturbed. I'd wake up with spazzing back pain. I'd try and get some ice packs just to like buy me another couple of hours of sleep," she added.

Base said even after her brother, who lives in Australia, was diagnosed with the condition, she was dismissed by doctors who told her it was not common in women.

It was a full 10 years after her symptoms that Base was given an MRI scan which proved she had axSpA.

She now controls the symptoms with bi-weekly injections.

"I was happy to be able to put a name to it, to be able to say to people 'I actually have this condition, not a random bad back'".

Even after "multiple visits to multiple GP surgeries over the years," she said: "I'd have hoped to have been taken seriously" "not dismissed."

Base said she believed a lack of awareness of the condition resulted in her waiting for a diagnosis for so long.

Delays to diagnosis for the condition are not uncommon.

According to analysis undertaken for NASS using data from the National Early Inflammatory Autoimmune Diseases Audit (NEIAA), even when they seek medical help, people in the UK wait an average of eight and a half to nine years to receive a diagnosis after symptoms first appear.

It also found that patients in the south west of England had an average delay in diagnosis of 9.2 years.

In the Bath and Bristol areas, the average diagnostic delay was even higher at 10.6 years.

Dr Dale Webb from the National Axial Spondyloarthritis Society (NASS) said GPs are not generally looking for inflammatory arthritis in young people so will not suspect axSpa.

"It is a very painful and progressive condition," he added.

Dr Elizabeth Reilly and Dr Sarah Villar, consultant rheumatologists with Bristol NHS Foundation Trust, said a multifaceted approach was needed to try to drive down the delay to diagnosis.

"We've been working really closely in Bristol and Bath with a project to collaborate together, as well as educating our local GPs and healthcare practitioners," said Reilly.

The duo have also been running a public awareness campaign via billboards at train stations, buses, and at universities, encouraging young people to think about their back pain.

Webb from NASS said an early diagnosis does not just save individuals from unnecessary suffering, it also helps the NHS and wider economy and said it "should be possible to diagnose someone within 12 months of their symptoms starting".

Webb said it would save the economy £3.1bn per year, "keep people in work" and decrease the need of people needing "to use the NHS so much".

While other joints can be affected, Axial spondyloarthritis (axSpA) is a form of arthritis that mostly causes pain and swelling in the spine and joints that connect the bottom of the spine to the pelvis.

According to the Arthritis Foundation , it is a systemic disease which can affect other body parts and organs and tends to run in families.

There are two types - ankylosing spondylitis (As), also known as radiographic axSpA, and nonradiographic axSpA (nr-axSpA).

The disease can affect people of any age but typically begins between the ages of 20 and 40.

Pain in the lower back, buttocks and hips

Pain, swelling, redness and warmth in the toes, heels, ankles, rib cage, knees, shoulders, spine and neck

Stiffness when first waking up or after long periods of rest

Back pain during the night or early morning

Children may have pain in the hips, knees or heels before the back.

Tendons and ligaments which attach to certain bones can also get inflamed and over a period of time can lead to bone forming.

articles.title: Survey finds 'major increase' in Channel Islands' cost of living
articles.summary: More than two thirds of respondents reported noticing rises in the cost of living.
articles.body:
There has been "a major increase" in the overall cost of living in the past 12 months in Guernsey, Jersey and the Isle of Man, a survey has found.

Island Global Research, a market research and consultancy company, found more than 69% of respondents in Jersey, 68% in Guernsey and 70% in the Isle of Man said they had noticed a cost increase .

The survey, which was completed by over 1,000 people in each island, saw 57% of respondents describe themselves as "less than comfortable" with about one in 10 going without essentials like food and heating.

The survey also found 65% said they now spent less on non essentials and 53% said they are shopping around more because of the price rises.

In Jersey, 10% of respondents reported they could not afford the increased costs and often have to go with out essentials, while in Guernsey it was 11%.

The survey also showed that two thirds of people in Jersey said they had found it difficult to meet living costs in the last 12 months, an increase of 17 percentage points compared to 2024 .

Guernsey also saw an increase with 58% reporting they found it difficult to meet living costs.

The survey also found about one in four received support to help finance their everyday living expenses in the last six months.

On the Isle of Man, 36% said they cut back on groceries and 30% received support to help finance everyday living expenses over a six-month period.

articles.title: Clarkson's choir 'so excited' for Royal Variety Performance
articles.summary: The Hawkstone Farmers' Choir are performing in the Royal Variety Performance on Friday evening.
articles.body:
A member of Jeremy Clarkson's Hawkstone Farmers' Choir has told the BBC he is "very excited" to sing at the Royal Variety Performance on Friday night.

The ensemble, which won Britain's Got Talent earlier this year , will sing in front of the King and Queen as part of the annual show - taking place this year at the Royal Albert Hall.

They are joined on the bill by Italian opera sensation Andrea Bocelli, singer-songwriter turned Celebrity Traitors sleuth James Blunt and the West End cast of Wicked.

Choir member David Smith, who lives near Banbury in Oxfordshire, said he was "very excited" for the performance.

"If someone had said to me a year ago that I would have won Britain's Got Talent and would be singing in front of His Majesty the King, I would have said 'oh look there's some pigs flying across the sky'," he said.

Looking ahead to Friday's Royal Variety Performance, Smith explained: "We've had a little bit of a taster because we did the National Television Awards, and on the front row were the kings and queens of television."

Smith had spent 45 years performing on the amateur stage in and around Oxfordshire before joining the choir.

"When you're used to singing at the Mill Banbury or Middleton Cheney Village Hall it's very weird, but so exciting," he said.

"Walking out onto that stage in front of all those people, it is what it is," Smith said of Friday's performance.

"There's no time for apprehension and nerves, you've just got to get on with it."

"It will be over in a flash - literally three minutes and it's done - and afterwards you just want to go back and wish you could do it again."

The performance coincides with the groups first album and comes hot on the heels of its first single, Absolution - which was released last month .

Describing the song, Oxfordshire-based choir member choir member James Florey said it was a "recognition of the daily grind" farmers go through.

"It's about letting that weight daily life fall away for a while, stepping away from it, and finding your space away from the pressures of everyday life," he added.

The choir was initially founded by Clarkson as part of an advertising campaign for his Cotswolds-based brewing firm, but has since used its platform to help raise awareness around mental health in farming.

In May, the group won the ITV talent show and received a £250,000 cash prize, as well as the chance to perform at the Royal Variety Performance.

articles.title: Remember Monday 'still feel nerves' after Eurovision
articles.summary: Life is an adrenaline rush for the trio after their rise to fame through the 2025 Eurovision final.
articles.body:
Remember Monday used to say that representing the UK at the 2025 Eurovision Song Contest was the "scariest" moment of their career.

But an upcoming album and UK tour will send the adrenaline soaring again, according to members Holly-Anne Hull, Charlotte Steele and Lauren Byrne.

"We still feel nerves like it all the time," Hull told BBC Introducing.

The vocal trio have recorded a new session for the programme, which was the first to play their music on the radio in 2019.

Seven years on, their credits include festivals, singles and the Eurovision final, where they came 19th out of 28 countries.

"We're always feeling nerves like it," Hull said.

"About a month later, we were performing at Wembley Stadium and we were like, 'I can't take it'," Byrne recalled.

"How can you possibly feel nerves like that again?"

The gig, in front of 80,000 people, led to a high-profile 2026 tour with pop-rock group McFly.

"Our dressing room was next to theirs at Wembley Stadium," Hull told presenter Steph Nieuwenhuys on BBC Introducing Hampshire, Dorset and the Isle of Wight.

"We just hit it off... We just toured the whole summer with them. Their crowds are crazy.

"It's scary being launched brand new into this industry without really knowing what we were doing.

"They've kind of taken us under their wing and been like: 'We'll look after you, you've got this.'"

Remember Monday's debut album, Can We Press Rewind?, is another "terrifying-slash-exciting" moment, according to Byrne.

Pre-released singles include the latest, Dream Cheat, a playful riff on the "relatable" experience of having a nightmare that a partner has been unfaithful.

The close-harmony trio met at The Sixth Form College in Farnborough, Hampshire.

Steele went on to be a founding member of performing arts sixth form Artemis College, in Bracknell, Berkshire, while all three have experience of performing in West End theatre shows.

Can We Press Rewind? is due for release on 29 January.

The group's six-city UK tour in February includes dates in Bristol, Birmingham, London, Portsmouth, Manchester and Glasgow.

articles.title: Poker popularity growing in Fenland, says league organiser
articles.summary: A poker league in Fenland sees a 35% rise in players since 2022.
articles.body:
A man who organises social poker sessions in pubs and clubs said the game's growing popularity could be down to the cost-of-living crisis.

Phillip Steer, from March, Cambridgeshire, has run poker nights in Fenland for 14 years and said he has seen a 35% rise in the number of players in the area since 2022, with now about "100 players across 15 clubs and pubs".

Steer added that as people can only place a maximum £5 stake, the game was often "cheaper" than other pastimes.

Player Violet Cunningham said: "I have been playing poker for about 10 years; it's nice to get out of the house... it's fun and exciting."

Tom Brady, the director of Live Pub Poker League (LPPL), said he had also seen an increase in the number of players joining for social tournaments in pubs and venues post-Covid, with the past 12 months being particularly busy.

On a chilly November evening about 15 people congregated in a pub in March, where they are given the use of a warm side room to set up their poker tables, cards and chips.

Steer said all sorts of people get involved in the game, adding: "We have men, women, retired and working people."

He said most people treat the game as a bit of fun and he did not worry that players would get into debt by taking part, due to the low-value stake.

"You buy 12,000 chips at the start of the night for £5 and once those have gone it is game over," he added.

Donald Rofe is a widower and lives alone in March, he said his family live in Wisbech and Cambridge.

"[Poker] gets me out of the house, although I have recently had my cataracts done, so I have some issues with reading the cards properly," he said.

Rofe admitted that he mistook a diamond for a heart, which cost him a victory.

"I put in all my chips because I thought I had a flush but I didn't, but it was still fun", he added.

The cost of play is another bonus for Rofe, who added he normally has one soft drink that will "last me all night".

Violet Cunningham is a full-time carer and said she liked to relax by playing poker.

"I have been playing poker for about 10 years, it's nice to get out of the house - it makes your brain tick, it's fun and exciting, but can be frustrating," she said.

Cunningham said she and her family grew up playing card games on holiday and she has always enjoyed playing them.

"I think women are harder to read than the men, play a bit tighter, unless they have it [a good hand] they probably won't bet on it," she added.

The Gambling Commission said that pub poker was classed as "exempt gaming" and can be carried out without a gambling licence or permit.

Players cannot place a stake more than £5 and combined stakes for the premises hosting the game cannot exceed £100 per day.

articles.title: Owen Cooper stars in The Beatles' In My Life music video
articles.summary: The film follows a family's love of music across generations and features Liverpool landmarks.
articles.body:
Award-winning actor Owen Cooper has starred in a new music video for The Beatles song In My Life.

The video for the newly mixed track, from the band's 1965 album Rubber Soul, celebrates their hometown of Liverpool.

The Warrington-born star appears in the film, which features Liverpool landmarks including the Royal Liver Building, Liverpool Cathedral, Royal Albert Dock and Strawberry Field.

Cooper, 16, is best known for his role in Netflix drama Adolescence, for which he won an Emmy Award.

Directed by Jessica Swale and Irina Alexiu, the video tells the story of a ukulele that connects generations of one family through a shared love of music.

A scene outside Woolton Picture House pays tribute to the band's famous Abbey Road album cover, while another recalls George Harrison's fall in the opening sequence of A Hard Day's Night.

Owen Cooper previously paid tribute to John Lennon and The Beatles as he collected a Bafta Television Award for Adolescence in May 2026.

Collecting the trophy, he said: "This is a bit mad.

"In the words of John Lennon, you won't get anything unless you have the vision to imagine it."
