articles.title: Patient, 83, waited nearly two days in chair at Lincoln A&E, son says
articles.summary: NHS apologises after patients and families describe "awful" conditions at Lincoln County Hospital.
articles.body:
The son of an 83-year-old cancer patient says she spent almost two days in a chair at A&E while waiting for a bed in hospital.

Nigel Wass says he had to bring his mother fluids, turn off alarms and find a wheelchair to take her to the toilet during "close to 48 hours" at Lincoln County Hospital, because staff were "run ragged".

One in 20 patients using Lincolnshire's emergency departments waited longer than 12 hours for a hospital bed, according to NHS figures for the year to October.

United Lincolnshire Teaching Hospitals NHS Trust (ULTH) apologised and said it "continued to implement improvements", including more rapid patient assessment and "timely patient discharges" to "free up beds".

Wass's mother had multiple infections during 18 months of cancer treatment, all needing emergency treatment.

He says he accompanied her to Lincoln County Hospital seven times between May and August and the emergency department was overwhelmed on each occasion.

On a visit in the summer, he says his mother was put in a chair in a side room, because she is immunosuppressed, but then forgotten about.

"The staff on the ground were amazing but there's simply not enough of them, so I'm caring for mum best I can, taking her to the toilet," Wass recalls.

"Fresh water wasn't available because the drinks machine has been broken for months. There are people in there that are dehydrated and that was the same with my mum.

"She had a drip, often the alarm would be going off it and it would take ages to get somebody to just come and press the reset button. In the end I did ask how to do it myself."

He describes his experience of the department as "crazy", with people "crying and afraid", lying on the floor, or "screaming in agony".

Paul Grantham-Rae says he was "absolutely disgusted" by his 85-year-old mother's experience at Lincoln's emergency department last month, after she spent 25 hours in a chair, then another seven sitting on a ward before a bed was found.

He says his mother had a leg wound, but because she takes blood thinners, the bandage was soon soaked and blood dripped on to the floor.

"We were asking the nurses if they could come and change it, and they said 'yes we'll be there shortly, we'll be there shortly," he recalls.

He says when he asked if staff knew how much blood she had lost, a nurse replied it was "a question we need to ask".

"I thought that's something that should have been detected straight away.

"There was one stage where her lips were quite blue."

Other patients and family members have told the BBC about similar experiences at Lincoln County Hospital. They include:

A man brought in by ambulance having a heart attack, who spent almost two days in a chair in the emergency department and waited five days for a bed on the cardiac ward.

A woman with a spinal fluid leak who spent 32 hours in a chair before being transferred to a specialist unit.

The daughter of an elderly woman with suspected sepsis, who says a nurse told everyone in the waiting area to go home, as the department was full.

NHS figures show the scale of pressure on emergency departments at Lincoln County and Boston Pilgrim hospitals.

The two departments saw 264,017 people in the year to October, with 5.2% waiting more than 12 hours to be admitted.

Fuelling the backlogs are delays in discharging patients who no longer need a bed. The figures show an average of 191 patients a day no longer required care in Lincoln, Boston and Grantham hospitals, but could not leave because of delays in social and community care, family arrangements, or organising medication.

Caroline Landon, the group chief operating officer at ULTH, says the trust's teams work "tirelessly" to monitor and care for those waiting to be admitted.

"Our hospitals, like many others in the country, are continuing to experience significant demand.

"During September alone, our A&E teams saw approximately 1,000 more patients compared to the previous September."

She says ULTH has "continued to implement improvements", including "quicker access to same-day emergency care" and "more rapid assessment" for those needing admission.

According to Landon, the trust is also "working closely with our Lincolnshire system partners to support timely patient discharges and improved access to community or home-based care, so that we free up beds in our hospitals".

Another patient frustrated by long waits is Martin Gibbs, who went to Lincoln's A&E with chest pains in October, two days after a heart procedure.

He says he spent 20 hours in a chair, waiting for an electrocardiogram and was not given his regular medication, as A&E staff were unable to access his records.

According to Gibbs, he was only given pain relief once, because a doctor in A&E signed him off to the cardiology unit, despite there being "no chance of getting me a bed".

He left after his partner, Nikki Applewhite, booked an electrocardiogram at a private hospital.

Applewhite says the department was "just awful".

"There was a man sitting there, it looked like his jaw was broken and he was bleeding. He just had a basket to catch the blood. There were two people either side of him on drips, both were bleeping, which obviously needed attending to.

"The water machine had broken, the vending machine had broken, the phone charging machine had broken.

"We talked to so many people and they said 'oh it's always like this' and you think, and you accept that that's normal?"

A spokesperson for the Department of Health and Social Care spokesperson said: "October was the busiest month ever for A&E, but thanks to the hard work of NHS staff, almost three quarters of people were seen within four hours."

CORRECTION, 20 November 2026: An earlier version of this article stated: "He says he spent 20 hours in a chair, waiting for an echocardiogram (ECG)." This should have stated electrocardiogram. This has been corrected.

articles.title: Nigeria suicide bill: Bola Tinubu moves to end jail terms for attempted suicide
articles.summary: Nigeria's proposed reform follows years of calls from psychiatrists and a parallel Senate bill.
articles.body:
Nigerian President Bola Tinubu has asked parliament to decriminalise attempted suicide, proposing medical support instead of prosecution for those who survive.

The proposal seeks to shift Nigeria's approach from criminal punishment to treatment and rehabilitation.

It follows years of calls for reform from mental health professionals. A separate bill seeking to decriminalise attempted suicide has already passed its second reading in the Senate.

Under Nigeria's law, attempted suicide is a criminal offence with those convicted facing up to one year's imprisonment, a fine or both.

The Senate bill also seeks to replace criminal penalties for attempted suicide with medical treatment, rehabilitation and support.

It was sponsored by Senator Asuquo Ekpenyong, who has argued that prosecuting people who survive suicide attempts could discourage those experiencing suicidal thoughts from seeking help.

He also warned that families might conceal such incidents for fear of prosecution and social stigma.

He stressed that the bill is not aimed at legalising or encouraging suicide attempts but rather protecting the survivors.

Tinubu's proposal has been welcomed by Senate President Godswill Akpabio, who had previously suggested that people who survived suicide attempts should be sent to prison.

"We are saying that suicide is a crime for now. Therefore, if you attempt it, we will send you to prison," Akpabio had said.

However, after receiving the Tinubu's proposal, he sought to clarify his earlier remarks, saying they did not apply to people experiencing mental health conditions.

He added that punishing people whose actions were influenced by mental health conditions would be insensitive.

Tinubu's letter follows sustained calls from mental health professionals for the law to be changed.

At a parliamentary public hearing in May 2024, the then president of the Association of Psychiatrists of Nigeria, Professor Taiwo Obindo, urged lawmakers to remove criminal penalties for attempted suicide.

"Why do we, as a nation, then punish individuals who are ill and need medical attention rather than prosecution?" he asked.

Drawing on his experience as a psychiatrist, Obindo said most people who die by suicide have a history of mental illness.

Akpabio has referred the president's amendment bill to the relevant senate committee for further consideration.

Nigeria is among several African countries where attempted suicide remains a criminal offence.

Ghana decriminalised attempted suicide in 2023, while Kenya's High Court ruled in January 2025 that the law criminalising it was unconstitutional.

articles.title: UK weather: Temperatures to drop to -10C on coldest night of autumn
articles.summary: Friday night is expected to be the coldest of the autumn so far with temperatures dropping as low as minus 10C, as Simon King explains.
articles.body:
The UK will experience the coldest night of autumn so far overnight on Friday, with a widespread frost developing as temperatures plummet below zero.

It will be particularly cold in northern areas, where temperatures of minus 1 (30F) to minus 5C (23F) are widely expected from the Midlands northward.

However, in rural areas of Scotland where there is some lying snow, it could get as low as minus 10C (14F).

It will stay cold with more overnight frost over the weekend, with cold health alerts from the UK's Health Security Agency remaining in force across northern England until Monday morning.

The coldest night of the autumn so far was on Thursday night when the temperature got down to minus 8.4C (18F) at Tulloch Bridge, Highland.

Temperatures for many of us have been up and down recently due to cold Arctic air temporarily sweeping southward across the UK.

Southern areas of the UK have mostly held onto milder air from the Atlantic.

During Friday though a northerly wind will once again bring some of the colder air from the Arctic, and bring a colder day for most of the UK.

Any early cloud and rain in southern England will clear and for most of the UK it will be a bright day with some sunshine. A few wintry showers are possible across Scotland.

By night, temperatures will drop with frost expected widely, mostly across the Midlands, northern England, Northern Ireland and Scotland.

Although it is likely to be the coldest night of the autumn so far, with minus 10C predicted in rural Scotland, we are a long way off the coldest November night on record, when a temperature of minus 16.1C was recorded in Cumbria in 1912.

We came closer to that record low temperature in 2025, when the UK experienced the coldest November night in 12 years with minus 12.6C in Moray.

How to keep babies warm in cold weather and other winter tips

How to look after dogs, cats and other pets in cold weather

Heating tips to keep your home warm when budgets are squeezed

After a cold start on Saturday morning, there will be a lot of dry and mostly sunny weather across the UK.

But milder air will start to move into the south-west of England again along with areas of cloud and rain by the end of the day.

Saturday night will not be as cold for most but frost is still likely to cover large areas of north-east England and much of Scotland with temperatures widely dropping to between zero and minus 5C.

Rain will continue on Sunday in south-west England, south Wales and even into parts of Northern Ireland.

Elsewhere should be mostly dry and while fairly cloudy, there should be some brighter interludes.

Maximum temperatures over the weekend will be on the colder side of average with 4 to 8C expected.

Is the polar vortex behind the cold weather?

The polar vortex is the strong wind that circles high above the Arctic.

Very unusually the winds of the polar vortex weakened last week - the earliest time this has happened on record .

In some situations, the weakening of the polar vortex can lead to colder weather and even snow some weeks later.

But it is too soon for this weakening of the polar vortex to be having an influence on our weather.

Instead this colder snap is just part of the variability of weather in the UK.

The polar vortex has started to strengthen again and should get back to its normal strength in the coming weeks.

Scientists are still unsure how or if the weakening last week will have any influence on our weather in weeks to come.

articles.title: EU and Britain to agree steps towards relations reset
articles.summary: A decade after Brexit, London is signalling a willingness to align more closely with the EU on various policies.
articles.body:
British and European Union leaders are set to meet at a summit billed as a chance to reset relations a decade after the Brexit vote.

UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham will meet with European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen and Antonio Costa, who heads the European Council, on Friday in Brussels . In the second such meeting since Britain formally left the bloc in 2020, deals on food, emissions and youth mobility are expected to be sealed.

The previous summit in 2025 was billed as a “stable foundation” upon which to rebuild the relationship between London and Brussels. Friday’s meeting is being sold as a chance to start on a reset of relations.

Burnham said earlier in the week that it was an “obvious truth” that Britain had lost more than it had gained from Brexit, which followed a non-binding referendum in 2016 in which 52 percent of the British public voted to leave the EU. He has signalled that a reformed relationship with Brussels is on his agenda.

The most valuable agreement on the table concerns the cross-border exchange of animals, plants and related products. Britain has estimated that the removal of the current controls could be worth 5.1 billion pounds ($6.7bn) annually.

A potential deal on emissions trading systems could see London and Brussels mutually exempt each other from carbon border levies on goods like steel.

An agreement on youth mobility, which would allow 100,000 people from the EU to live and work for up to three years in the UK, and vice versa, is also reportedly set to be signed. The UK had originally wanted half that number.

The EU is also pushing for students to qualify for “home fees” at British universities – often one third of the international price. London, however, has only agreed to apply “significantly reduced” fees.

The UK also wants to be part of the EU’s “Made in Europe” rules. Brussels has said it may be open to this, but it would require the UK to accept its policies. That could prove tricky for Burnham, given that the UK still hosts a significant Eurosceptic population.

Nigel Farage, leader of the populist radical right-wing Reform UK party, accused Burnham of a Brexit “betrayal”.

“We don’t need to be in political union of any kind at all to do business and have good relations with our neighbours,” he told the BBC. “I’m afraid that the great Brexit debate has just started again.”

articles.title: A Frida Kahlo painting expected to sell for up to $3.5 million was withdrawn from a Christie’s auction in New York just hours before bidding, after questions emerged over its ownership and how it left Mexico
articles.summary: A rare painting by Mexican artist Frida Kahlo was withdrawn from a high-profile Christie’s auction in New York shortly before it was due to go under the
articles.body: A rare painting by Mexican artist Frida Kahlo was withdrawn from a high-profile Christie’s auction in New York shortly before it was due to go under the hammer, following concerns over its ownership history and whether it had been legally removed from Mexico. The development, reported by Smithsonian Magazine and El País, has brought renewed attention to the fate of artworks from Kahlo’s historic collection and the responsibility of auction houses to establish their provenance before a sale. The painting, Congreso de los pueblos por la paz (Congress of the Peoples for Peace), was created in 1952 and had been expected to fetch between $2.5 million and $3.5 million at Christie’s 20th Century Evening Sale on November 17, 2026. Its withdrawal came after Mexican cultural authorities sought further information about its ownership and the circumstances surrounding its departure from the country.Why the painting’s ownership is being questionedThe controversy centres on the painting’s connection to Casa Azul, the Mexico City home where Kahlo was born, lived for much of her life and died in 1954. The house was later converted into the Frida Kahlo Museum. According to the group Defendamos la Colección Gelman, the painting appears in an inventory prepared by Kahlo’s husband, fellow artist Diego Rivera, in 1957, when arrangements were made to preserve the couple’s belongings for the Mexican public. Rivera had intended the Casa Azul collection to remain a cultural legacy for the country.The group’s concerns are supported by Pedro Diego Alvarado, Rivera’s grandson, who has also placed the painting among the works and possessions kept at Kahlo’s studio in Casa Azul. The questions surrounding the artwork gained momentum after Hilda Trujillo, former director of the Frida Kahlo Museum, raised concerns in 2025 about discrepancies between the museum’s historical inventory and the artworks that were eventually accounted for. Her research pointed to several paintings and other works that appeared to have entered private collections, including Congreso de los pueblos por la paz. Trujillo also questioned how these works had left the museum’s collection and who had authorised their transfer.The disputed journey from Mexico to private collectionsThe painting’s movements over the decades have become central to the investigation. Mexican authorities initially maintained that the artwork had left the country in 1952, when it was taken to Vienna, Austria, for the Congress of the Peoples for Peace. The painting was created in connection with the gathering, which brought together artists, writers and intellectuals advocating peace.However, its subsequent history has raised questions. Christie’s records indicate that the painting returned to Mexico in 1953 and was displayed at Kahlo’s first solo exhibition in April that year, held at the Galería de Arte Contemporáneo in Mexico City.Historical accounts also suggest that Rivera and his daughter, architect Ruth Rivera Marín, took the painting to Europe, as Kahlo’s deteriorating health prevented her from travelling. The artwork’s next documented public appearances came decades later. It featured in an exhibition in Madrid and Barcelona in 1997 and was subsequently included in a touring exhibition in Japan between 2003 and 2004.By 1988, however, the painting had already been identified in records as belonging to a private collection. It was later offered through a New York gallery before appearing at Sotheby’s in 2020, eventually entering the hands of a private collector. The gap between its return to Mexico in 1953 and its later appearance in private ownership is one of the central issues that investigators are seeking to clarify.What Mexican authorities have saidMexico’s National Institute of Fine Arts and Literature (INBAL) has requested documentation from Christie’s to establish the painting’s provenance and legal ownership. The institute is also coordinating with the Diego Rivera and Frida Kahlo Museum Trust, whose trustee is the Bank of Mexico. The legal position is particularly important. In 1984, Kahlo’s entire artistic output was declared an artistic monument under Mexican law. While the designation does not prohibit the domestic sale of her paintings, it restricts their permanent export from Mexico.INBAL’s initial position was that the painting had left the country before the 1984 decree came into effect. However, the documented return for Kahlo’s 1953 exhibition has complicated the question of when it actually left Mexico permanently. The Frida Kahlo Museum has confirmed that the painting is included in an ongoing investigation involving several artworks. Authorities are examining the available documentation as they seek to establish the circumstances surrounding the pieces’ ownership and movement.Christie’s subsequently confirmed that the decision to withdraw the painting was taken in agreement with its seller to allow further research. The auction house has indicated that it hopes to offer the work for sale at a later date, although no fresh auction date has been announced. For now, the painting remains at the centre of a wider debate about the preservation of Mexico’s artistic heritage, the protection of museum collections and the documentation required when historically significant works enter the international art market.You use AI every day. articles.title: Hours after Putin's 'painful' revenge warning, Russia unleashes massive attack on Ukraine
articles.summary: Russia launched a massive overnight missile and drone attack on Ukraine, killing at least three people in Kyiv, knocking out power in parts of the capital
articles.body: Russia launched a massive overnight missile and drone attack on Ukraine, killing at least three people in Kyiv, knocking out power in parts of the capital and damaging key transport infrastructure. The strikes came hours after Russian president Vladimir Putin vowed a “much more painful” response to Ukrainian attacks on the bridge linking Russia to the annexed Crimean peninsula.Kyiv mayor Vitali Klitschko confirmed the casualties in a post on Telegram on Friday. “At present, 3 people are known to have been killed,” he wrote, adding that at least 15 others had been wounded.Three bridges crossing the Dnipro river were also hit, threatening further disruption to daily life in the Ukrainian capital. AFP journalists reported hearing explosions through the night, while unofficial monitoring services reported that as many as three dozen missiles were in Ukrainian airspace at one point.According to news agency Reuters, Russia’s defence ministry confirmed on Friday that its forces had carried out a “massive” attack using missiles and drones. It said the strikes targeted defence industry facilities, as well as energy and transport infrastructure, in several regions of Ukraine, including Kyiv.In its statement, the ministry said Russian forces had hit road and rail bridges in Kyiv that were used to transport weapons and military equipment to the battlefield. It also reported strikes on port infrastructure in the Odesa region and vessels allegedly used for Ukrainian military purposes.The ministry later said Russian forces had struck a cargo vessel carrying military equipment to the port of Odesa. These claims could not be independently verified.Attacks were also reported in the western regions of Lviv and Ivano-Frankivsk, while a hospital was struck in the northeastern city of Kharkiv. One person was also killed in the southern Zaporizhzhia region.Putin vows retaliation over Crimean bridge strikesThe latest assault followed Putin’s warning during his visit to China, where he met Chinese president Xi Jinping and US president Donald Trump. Speaking after the meetings, the Russian leader said Moscow’s response to Ukrainian strikes on the Crimean bridge would be “much more painful”.Ukrainian attacks earlier this week severed the highway section of the road-and-rail link, according to satellite images published by imaging firm Vantor. The 19 km bridge, which connects Russia to the Crimean peninsula, annexed by Moscow in 2014, has remained a key target during the war.The overnight strikes followed further attacks on Kyiv on Thursday, when a landmark cathedral and several foreign embassies sustained damage. The Austrian, Brazilian and Dutch embassies reported light damage after drones struck the city.Ukraine war diplomacy remains stalledMeanwhile, efforts to negotiate an end to the conflict have shown little progress, with Moscow maintaining its demands. Putin has said any settlement must form part of a wider agreement on European security and described Ukraine-Europe military cooperation as a “problem”.He also said Russia had invited European representatives to Moscow to discuss their position before deciding whether they could join negotiations. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky called it a “mistake” for European leaders to travel to Moscow, while insisting they should be included in talks held elsewhere.German chancellor Friedrich Merz said Europe must have a seat at the negotiating table.Separately, Ukraine’s Unmanned Systems Forces commander Robert “Magyar” Brovdi said Ukrainian forces had struck 40 Russian oil facilities and defence industry targets over the past 50 days.You use AI every day. articles.title: Islam set to be the largest religion by 2035: Where will most Muslims live?
articles.summary: Pew Research projects Muslim population in Pakistan will overtake Indonesia by 2070, with India next and Nigeria third.
articles.body:
Muslims are projected to outnumber Christians worldwide by 2035, according to projections released by the Pew Research Center .

Both religions will keep growing. Between 2020 and 2070, the number of Muslims is expected to rise by 80 percent, from 2.02 billion to 3.64 billion. Christians are projected to grow by 30 percent to 2.96 billion, roughly in step with the world population.

Muslims are projected to grow faster than any other major religious group. Hindus and Jews are expected to grow more slowly than the world population, while the number of Buddhists and people with no religion is projected to shrink.

The main reason is birth rates. Between 2020 and 2025, Muslim women had an average of 3.1 children, compared with 2.5 for Christian women and 1.6 for all other women. A population needs about 2.1 children per woman to replace itself.

Births minus deaths are projected to add 1.6 billion Muslims and 792 million Christians by 2070.

Which countries will have the most Muslims?

Most of the growth will happen where Muslims are already the majority. The 53 Muslim-majority countries are expected to gain 1.2 billion Muslims by 2070, 74 percent of the global increase.

Indonesia had the world’s largest Muslim population in 2020, at 239 million. Pakistan, just 12 million behind, is projected to take the top spot. Pew’s figures compare 2020 with 2070, so they do not say exactly when, but with Pakistan’s Muslim population set to double to 461 million while Indonesia’s grows 15 percent, the switch is likely to come well before 2070.

By 2070, India’s Muslim population is projected to rise from third to second, growing from 213 million to 334 million. Nigeria jumps from fifth to third, more than doubling to 282 million and pushing Indonesia to fourth.

Four of the top 10 in 2070 are in Africa: Nigeria, Egypt, Ethiopia and Sudan. Ethiopia and Afghanistan join the list, replacing Iran and Algeria, while Sudan’s Muslim population more than doubles to 116 million and climbs above Turkiye.

Pew’s projections cover 201 countries and territories, home to 99.98 percent of the world’s population. They assume current trends in fertility, mortality and religious switching continue, and could change with wars, disasters or economic shifts.

articles.title: India, Malaysia begin Harimau Shakti military drill with focus on counter-terror ops
articles.summary: The sixth edition of the India-Malaysia joint military exercise Harimau Shakti began on Friday at Ipoh in Malaysia, with 120 personnel from each side
articles.body: The sixth edition of the India-Malaysia joint military exercise Harimau Shakti began on Friday at Ipoh in Malaysia, with 120 personnel from each side taking part. The exercise, a bilateral training event held alternately in the two countries, will run till November 30.The stated aim is to rehearse sub-conventional operations under Chapter VII of the United Nations mandate, with particular emphasis on synergising responses during counter-terrorism missions. The two armies will work in jungle and semi-urban terrain, relying on joint planning, tactical coordination and emerging technologies to improve interoperability.The exercise will unfold in phases. In the first phase, troops will first undergo cross-training to familiarise themselves with each other's operating procedures, followed by joint tactical drills. These include setting up a Joint Command Post and Surveillance Centre, counter-terrorism operations, raids, cordon-and-search drills and combat engineering tasks. Special attention will go to Unmanned Aerial Systems for reconnaissance and surveillance, along with counter-drone capabilities to detect and neutralise hostile unmanned platforms. The exercise will end with a validation drill built around a simulated counter-terrorism scenario, combining ground operations, integrated surveillance and unmanned systems.The fifth edition was held last year at the Mahajan Field Firing Range in Rajasthan from December 5 to 18 last year. The Indian contingent then largely comprised troops from the Dogra Regiment, while Malaysia was represented by the 25th Battalion of the Royal Malaysian Army.The exercise reflects a wider deepening of defence ties. India and Malaysia established diplomatic relations in 1957 and a Memorandum of Understanding on Defence Cooperation signed in 1993 gave military engagement an institutional framework. The Joint Defence Cooperation Committee reviews existing cooperation and identifies new areas. In August 2024, the two countries elevated their ties to a Comprehensive Strategic Partnership.The naval dimension has grown as well. The fourth edition of Samudra Laksamana was held at Lumut from September 9 to 12 this year, with INS Mysore exercising alongside the Royal Malaysian Navy's KD Lekir and KD Gagah Samudera. In October 2025 INS Sahyadri visited Kemaman, while the survey vessel INS Sandhayak made a port call at Klang in July 2025. The navies of both nations also take part in multilateral platforms such as MILAN and the ASEAN-India Maritime Exercise.Defence manufacturing is emerging as another area of cooperation. India is looking to expand exports to Southeast Asia, while Malaysia seeks to modernise its forces and diversify its sources of procurement. Hindustan Aeronautics Limited, Mazagon Dock Shipbuilders, Bharat Dynamics Limited and BEML showcased their products at LIMA 2025. The two countries are also co-chairing the SEAN Defence Ministers' Meeting-Plus (ADMM) counter-terrorism working group for 2024-2027.

articles.title: ‘Let Students Search’: Google employees want an AI-free option for schools, here’s why
articles.summary: Hundreds of Google employees have signed a petition asking the company to give schools a version of Google Search without generative AI.
articles.body: Hundreds of Google employees have signed a petition asking the company to give schools a version of Google Search without generative AI. The appeal comes as three of the largest US school districts weigh switching search engines, according to The New York Times. The issue is whether schools can turn off AI for students and still let them look things up on Google.The dispute began earlier this month when Google’s vice president for education, Chris Phillips, told the Times that Search and AI were “deeply integrated”. He said students attempting to use Search at schools that ban AI would see a message saying the service was unavailable. Some districts, including New York City, have already restricted student-facing generative AI over concerns about how it affects learning.New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani accused Google of using its market power to push AI into public schools. In Chicago, parents, teachers and students protested outside a Google office. The Times subsequently reported that New York City, Los Angeles and Chicago were all considering alternative search engines.What Google workers are asking forThe Alphabet Workers Union’s petition, titled “Let Students Search”, is addressed to Phillips, Google CEO Sundar Pichai and Search chief Elizabeth Hamon Reid. The union argues that educators should decide when students use AI and that taking away Search could prompt districts to drop other Google products. It also warned that losing school district business could affect job security.“The decision of how and when to implement AI into a classroom belongs to the educators leading it,” Parul Koul, the union’s president and a Google software engineer, said in a statement.Can schools turn off AI inside SearchGoogle has said that under changes expected early next year, schools will be able to enable or disable Search, Gemini and NotebookLM individually. That means a school could switch off the standalone Gemini chatbot and keep Search available to students. Google’s clarification left open whether schools could also disable the generative AI features that appear within Search itself.The union said some coverage had made it sound as though Google was deliberately punishing schools for opting out of AI. Its petition asks for a setting that would let schools apply their classroom AI policies to Search while keeping the search engine available for everyday use.Fearless legend or grounded realist? articles.title: Massachusetts’ top court to hear Lindsay Clancy’s bid to toss murder charges
articles.summary: Massachusetts’ highest court said that it will hear arguments ‌in Lindsay Clancy’s bid to dismiss the murder charges stemming from the 2023 deaths of her three young children and avoid being tried a second time.
articles.body: BOSTON — Massachusetts’ highest court said on Thursday that it will hear arguments ‌in Lindsay Clancy’s bid to dismiss the murder charges stemming from the 2023 deaths of her three young children and avoid being tried a second time. Justice Elizabeth Dewar said review by the full Massachusetts Supreme Judicial Court was warranted and the case ​would be heard in January, ahead of Clancy’s planned March 29 retrial. Judge William Sullivan in Plymouth ​had scheduled the retrial during a hearing on Monday, a week after he rejected arguments that ⁠a second trial would run afoul of Clancy’s protection under the U.S. Constitution’s Fifth Amendment against being tried ​twice for the same crime, known as double jeopardy. Sullivan on September 4 declared a mistrial after the jury in her ​initial trial reported that a holdout juror was preventing it from reaching a unanimous verdict. Clancy’s lawyers in their appeal contend that the mistrial declaration had not been manifestly necessary. “We are pleased that the state supreme judicial court will receive briefs and ​hear oral argument on an issue of great importance — whether Ms Clancy’s constitutionally guaranteed double jeopardy rights prohibit ​a second prosecution,” defense attorney Martin Weinberg said in a statement. Clancy, 36, faces first-degree murder charges over the deaths of her ‌daughter ⁠Cora, 5; son Dawson, 3; and 8-month-old son Callan. If convicted of those charges, she would be sentenced to life in prison without parole. No one at Clancy’s initial trial disputed that she strangled the children with exercise bands on January 24, 2023, in the basement of their home in the Boston suburb of Duxbury. She then ​cut herself with a knife ​and jumped from a ⁠second-story window in an attempt to end her own life, leaving her paralyzed. Clancy’s lawyers have argued the evidence showed she was in the throes of postpartum psychosis when ​she killed her children and should be found not guilty by reason of ​insanity, known in ⁠Massachusetts as lack of criminal responsibility. Citing jury notes that stated the holdout juror was not following the law on reasonable doubt despite the judge’s instructions, defense lawyers in Clancy’s appeal said that rather than declare a mistrial, Sullivan ⁠should have ​instead questioned the holdout and potentially removed the juror. Plymouth County District ​Attorney Timothy Cruz’s office in a brief on Wednesday countered that the high court should reject Clancy’s appeal without a hearing so prosecutors ​could “continue to pursue justice for Cora, Dawson, and Callan Clancy.”

articles.title: Four men found guilty of sex crimes against U.K. woman in a case that recalls Gisèle Pelicot’s
articles.summary: Four British men were found guilty of multiple sexual crimes, including rape, against a woman whose then-husband drugged and advertised her for sex online, in a case that raised widespread comparisons to that of Gisèle Pelicot in France.
articles.body: LONDON — Four British men were found guilty Thursday of multiple sexual crimes, including rape, against a woman whose then-husband drugged and advertised her for sex online, in a case that raised widespread comparisons to that of Gisèle Pelicot in France. Joanne Young, who waived her right to anonymity as Pelicot had, spoke of her “relief” at the jury verdict and urged other women who have experienced anything similar to go to authorities in the knowledge that they “can be believed and understood.” “Knowing what has happened to me without my knowledge or consent has been incredibly difficult to process, and this abuse has cost me my life as I knew it,” she said outside Winchester Crown Court in southern England. “The person I trusted most in the world betrayed me in the most horrific way.” The 49-year-old mother of three spoke after the jury found the four men, whose ages range from 32 to 62, guilty of abusing her at her home in Swindon after being recruited on the internet. Her ex-husband, Philip Young, had previously pleaded guilty to dozens of offenses including 11 counts of rape and 11 of administering a substance with intent. Norman Macksoni, 48, was found guilty of one charge of rape. Richard Wilkins, 62, was found guilty of one count of rape and one of assault by penetration. Connor Sanderson-Doyle, 32, was convicted of sexual assault by penetration and sexual touching while Mohammed Hassan was found guilty of one count of sexual touching. A sixth defendant, Dean Hamilton, 47, admitted one charge of assault by penetration, two of sexual assault and one of rape. Justice Pushpinder Saini said the four men faced “significant” prison sentences and praised Joanne Young for her “amazing bravery throughout these proceedings.” Court had heard of 13 years of abuse The court heard that over a 13-year period, Philip Young, who served as a locally-elected official for the Conservative Party in Swindon between 2007 and 2010, drugged and raped his wife and invited other men on websites and apps such as Craigslist, Grindr and Fab Swingers to have sex with her without her knowledge. Joanne Young said her case raised “serious questions” over how the law deals with consent and urged the government to look into the issue to better protect women. “Consent has to come from the person themselves, no one should be able to give it on your behalf, and no one should be able to rely on someone else’s word that you agreed,” she said. “At no point did anyone ask me for my consent.” James Foster, specialist prosecutor for the Crown Prosecution Service, said the men found guilty “chose to commit unspeakable acts of abuse against Joanne Young without bothering to check if she was consenting.” Case had echoes of Gisèle Pelicot’s ordeal in France Domestic abuse charity Refuge said the guilty verdicts represented “long overdue justice” but “cannot undo the devastating abuse inflicted upon” Joanne Young. “Echoing the case of Gisèle Pelicot in 2024, the atrocities committed against Joanne by Philip Young and multiple other men are a clear reminder that, in the powerful words of Gisèle, shame must change sides,” it said. In December 2024, Pelicot’s ex-husband, Dominique Pelicot, and 50 other men were convicted of sexually assaulting her between 2011 and 2020 while she was under chemical submission. He was sentenced to 20 years in prison, while the other defendants received sentences ranging from three to 15 years. The shocking case of Pelicot and her decision to waive her anonymity and speak publicly prompted a reckoning over rape culture in France and beyond. Philip Young’s abuse came to light in July 2024, when the local Wiltshire Police force received information that an account on the free mobile messaging and livestreaming app Kik linked to him had uploaded three extreme bestiality images to the platform. Full searches of his devices then identified five videos showing Joanne incapacitated and tied to the bed at their shared home address as well as chat threads which showed that Young had shared intimate images of Joanne online without her knowledge. “It is hard to put into words the depth of Young’s exploitation and abuse of Jo,” said senior investigating officer detective superintendent Geoff Smith. “Young put her health at risk through deliberately drugging her without her knowledge and inviting strangers to rape her, depriving her of autonomy over her own body.” Joanne Young said she now never feels completely safe, but said that with the support of her loved ones she is “working hard to rebuild my life.”

articles.title: SC upholds Karnataka HC order to allow bike taxis, rejects state govt's challenge
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: In a setback to the Karnataka government, the Supreme Court on Friday refused to interfere with a state high court ruling that permits bike
articles.body: NEW DELHI: In a setback to the Karnataka government, the Supreme Court on Friday refused to interfere with a state high court ruling that permits bike taxi services to operate across Karnataka.A bench of Justices Satish Chandra Sharma and N Kotiswar Singh dismissed the state's appeal, thereby retaining the relief granted to bike taxi aggregators and operators by the Karnataka High Court, news agency ANI reported.The case dates back to an earlier order that had asked bike taxi operators to halt services until the state introduced a regulatory framework. However, on January 23, 2026, a division bench of the high court, then headed by Chief Justice Vibhu Bakhru and comprising Justice CM Joshi, overturned that direction.The high court's ruling came on appeals by Ola, Uber, Rapido, motorcycle owners and the Bike Taxi Welfare Association. It said motorcycles could be registered as transport vehicles and used as contract carriages, provided they complied with the state's regulatory requirements.The state government subsequently approached the apex court, arguing that the operation of bike taxis raised concerns about passenger safety, insurance protection and the absence of adequate safeguards.Traditional auto and taxi driver associations had also opposed the move, contending that bike taxi operators should not be allowed to function without meeting regulatory obligations comparable to those imposed on conventional transport services.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: Prosecutor declines to charge Wisconsin police officer who fatally shot a Black man
articles.summary: The Wisconsin police officer who shot and killed a 38-year-old Black man in Madison in July acted reasonably and will not face criminal charges, a prosecutor said Thursday, drawing immediate condemnation from the victim’s family members and community advocates.
articles.body: MADISON, Wis. — The Wisconsin police officer who shot and killed a 38-year-old Black man in Madison in July acted reasonably and will not face criminal charges, a prosecutor said Thursday, drawing immediate condemnation from the victim’s family members and community advocates. The shooting of Corey Ruiz, which was captured on video, sparked racial justice protests and calls for police reform. City leaders braced for more protests in the hours after the decision not to charge the officer, who is white. The victim’s brother, Adam Ruiz, told reporters the prosecutor had “mistreated” his family. “We’re destroyed,” he said. “We won’t accept this.” Dane County District Attorney Ismael Ozanne said Ruiz resisted officers, produced a knife and was unaffected by multiple Taser rounds immediately before officer Kiel Baitinger-Peterson shot and killed him on July 22. Under those circumstances, it was “reasonable for the officer to use deadly force,” and there was no “potential criminal court liability,” the district attorney concluded. Ozanne said he reached his decision after reviewing police reports, diagrams, surveillance videos, police squad car videos and citizen videos. Madison police officers do not wear body cameras. Family attorney blasts decision Civil rights attorney Ben Crump, who represents the Ruiz family, said there was nothing in the videos that justified the shooting. “In the video you see they tackle him, they tase him, they kick him and then the police officer executes him,” Crump said at a news conference, surrounded by Ruiz’s family. “The video is the objective unbiased witness here.” Crump said it is one of the worst cases of excessive force that he has worked on. “When you are shooting a man who is on the ground, three (times). It hits him in his chest and the kill shot hits him in his head,” he said. Crump said the medical examiner told the Ruiz family he would have survived had the third shot not been fired and hit him in the head. Ozanne said his decision was a correct interpretation of the law. “A person does not have to like and/or agree with the law, however I am sworn to apply the law to the facts at hand,” the prosecutor said. “The law applies equally to members of law enforcement and to those who are not.” A few dozen people gathered by late afternoon at the site of the shooting, which was marked by bouquets of flowers at the busy Madison intersection. After dark, a candlelight vigil was held. One person held a sign that said, “No justice, no peace, no racist police.” ‘He’s got a knife! He’s got a knife!’ Baitinger-Peterson did not immediately reply to an email seeking comment. He was one of four officers who responded to calls about someone checking out parked cars and an alleged burglary attempt on the day of the shooting, police said. They surrounded Ruiz, who was on a bicycle, in the middle of an intersection, tussling with him. In police dash-camera video released by the Wisconsin Department of Justice Thursday, officers repeatedly yell, “He’s got a knife! He’s got a knife!” The weapon is clearly visible in Ruiz’s right hand, the blade pointed downward, as a fourth officer arrives and deploys a Taser. Ruiz stumbles and falls onto his right side before Baitinger-Peterson fires three shots at close range. Baitinger-Peterson told investigators during an interview days after the shooting that he got on his knees and grabbed Ruiz’s right arm before realizing Ruiz was holding a knife, according to records released Thursday. He said he was struggling to control the arm and feared that Ruiz would stab the officers. He said he fired a third time because Ruiz’s facial expression and body did not change after the first two shots, leading him to believe they had not struck him. Documents show Baitinger-Peterson had minor injuries to both hands. Jim Palmer, executive director of the police union, the Wisconsin Professional Police Association, said the district attorney’s decision was “supported by the evidence and consistent with the legal standards governing the use of force by law enforcement officers.” It was the third time since 2012 that Madison police had shot and killed someone in the same neighborhood. Officials urge protesters to stay peaceful Baitinger-Peterson, who has more than a decade of experience in law enforcement, and the other three officers who interacted with Ruiz that day have been on paid administrative leave since the shooting. Madison Police Chief John Patterson said police will now conduct an internal review of the shooting. All of the officers involved will remain on administrative leave, he said. Wisconsin Gov.-elect David Crowley called for any protests to remain peaceful, though he said in a video statement that Ruiz’s killing was “deeply troubling.” Noting he was the state’s first Black governor-elect, he said such incidents were part of a longer history. “The decision not to file charges does not end the conversation or resolve the questions this tragedy has raised,” he said.

articles.title: U.N. top court’s landmark ruling on state-sponsored Rohingya genocide ‘unfair,’ Myanmar says
articles.summary: The United Nations’ highest court ruling ​that found Myanmar’s security forces conducted genocide against the country’s Rohingya Muslim minority was unfair.
articles.body: A ruling by the United Nations’ highest court ​that found Myanmar’s security forces conducted state-sponsored genocide against the country’s Rohingya Muslim minority was unfair, a government official said on Friday. The decision by the International Court of Justice was not unanimous and Myanmar had ⁠been unjustly accused, said Khaing Khaing Soe, a government spokesperson. The ruling was the first time the court has held a state responsible for genocide. It came seven years after the case was filed by predominantly Muslim Gambia. It was the fourth time since the Nazi ⁠Holocaust that an international court ruled that ​the ⁠legal threshold to prove genocide had been met. “Our country was unjustly accused,” Khaing Khaing Soe told a press conference in the capital Naypyitaw. “I want ⁠to say that this decision is not a unanimous decision by everyone, it ​is ⁠not fair.” Mass executions, widespread rape Judges ‌found that Myanmar’s military carried out mass executions of men and boys, committed widespread rape and sexual violence against Rohingya women and burned or razed hundreds ‌of villages during so-called clearance operations. Long persecuted in Buddhist-majority ‌Myanmar, the mainly Muslim Rohingya face escalating violence in their war-torn homeland and worsening conditions in crowded refugee camps in neighboring Bangladesh where 1.2 million of them live. The ruling said Myanmar had ⁠an obligation to compensate the Rohingya for the violations it had committed, to be determined later, and it must also allow the “safe and dignified return” of Rohingya displaced as a result of Myanmar’s “wrongful acts.” Thousands of Rohingya refugees living in sprawling camps in Bangladesh celebrated the verdict, but it remained unclear when they would be able to return home. While rulings by the ICJ, which settles disputes between states and ‌rules on alleged breaches of international treaties, are final, the court ​has very limited options to enforce them. The court’s 191-page judgment ‌also referenced a Reuters investigation into the ⁠killing of 10 Rohingya Muslims in Inn Din on September 7, 2017 ⁠and the subsequent arrest of two of its reporters, who were held for more than 500 ‌days. Asked for a response ​to the ruling, Khaing Khaing Soe ‌said major world leaders had previously said “political ​bodies” similar to the ICJ “should not abuse their judicial authority.”

articles.title: Petrol bombs, burning vehicles and 'murder bid': YSRCP accuses TDP supporters of attacking leaders in Tadipatri, Kadapa
articles.summary: ANANTAPUR: Tension prevailed in parts of Andhra Pradesh on Friday after the YSRCP accused supporters of the ruling TDP-led coalition of attacking the
articles.body: ANANTAPUR: Tension prevailed in parts of Andhra Pradesh on Friday after the YSRCP accused supporters of the ruling TDP-led coalition of attacking the residences and convoys of its leaders, including former MLA Kethireddy Peddareddy and Kadapa MP YS Avinash Reddy.In Tadipatri, the YSRCP alleged that supporters of TDP leader JC Prabhakar Reddy attacked the residence of former MLA Kethireddy Peddareddy and attempted to kill him.According to the party, the attackers hurled petrol bombs, damaged vehicles parked in Peddareddy's convoy and set them on fire. A generator on the ground floor of his residence was also allegedly set ablaze, news agency ANI reported.The party further accused the police of responding belatedly to the incident, claiming that personnel arrived at the location later and dispersed TDP supporters gathered near Peddareddy's house.Separately, tension erupted near Ankalamma Gudur in Simhadripuram of YSR Kadapa district when the convoy of YSRCP MP YS Avinash Reddy was allegedly targeted while he was travelling to extend support to party candidates during the nomination-filing process.According to the YSRCP state office, supporters of TDP MLC Ravi attacked the MP's convoy with stones and sticks and allegedly hurled petrol bombs at the vehicles. The party condemned the incident, raising concerns over the security of elected representatives and candidates participating in the electoral process.YSRCP national spokesperson Mahaboob Shareef accused TDP official spokesperson Ravi and his supporters of targeting Avinash Reddy's convoy with stones, petrol bombs, weapons and sticks. He alleged that the attack was a deliberate attempt to kill the MP."Suddenly, an attack was carried out on him, and an attempt was made to kill him," Shareef said, alleging that Ravi and his supporters were responsible.Calling the incident an assault on democratic institutions, Shareef said, "This is not just an attack on MP Avinash Reddy; it is an attack on the entire democracy. Such actions are not appropriate. Whatever the coalition government is doing is absolutely wrong."He also questioned the conduct of the police, alleging that personnel remained silent despite the seriousness of the incident and failed to intervene effectively. Shareef accused the coalition government of allowing political violence and intimidation to take place during the electoral process.Referring to directions issued by the high court and the Supreme Court, the YSRCP spokesperson said the apex court had instructed the Election Commission to ensure the safety and security of candidates. However, he alleged that the poll body had failed to implement the directions."The Election Commission has also become a puppet of the coalition government. This appears to be a well-planned conspiracy. A major conspiracy has been hatched to attempt to kill MP Avinash Reddy. YSRCP will not tolerate this," he said.The party maintained that candidates and elected representatives must be allowed to participate in the nomination process without threats or intimidation and accused the ruling coalition of failing to provide a safe environment for the democratic exercise.The latest allegations come against the backdrop of earlier complaints of electoral violence in the state. On November 1, YSRCP Kadapa MP YS Avinash Reddy had alleged violence and polling irregularities at several polling booths during Andhra Pradesh's urban local body elections."The polling for the municipal elections began this morning. There is violence at every polling booth. The TDP agents are taking away the slip, sending the voters outside and casting the votes of the common voters," he had alleged.Meanwhile, YSRCP polling agent Sunitha Pulivendula had also claimed that party agents were facing resistance while attempting to enter polling booths. She said she was trying to ensure that voters could exercise their franchise peacefully.The YSRCP has repeatedly raised concerns over the safety of its leaders, polling agents and candidates, alleging that incidents of intimidation and violence are affecting the electoral process in Andhra Pradesh.(With agency inputs)You Can Also Check: Gold Rate in Vijayawada | Silver Rate in Vijayawada | Bank Holidays in Vijayawada | Public Holidays in Vijayawada | Petrol Price in Vijayawada | Diesel Price in Vijayawada | CNG Price in Vijayawada | LPG Price in VijayawadaStay updated with the latest Vijayawada news. articles.title: An Egyptian writer who spent more than six years imprisoned won America's National Book Award for nonfiction, but could not attend the New York ceremony after US officials denied him a visitor visa
articles.summary: An Egyptian writer who spent more than six years in prison for his political activism has won one of America's biggest literary honours.
articles.body: An Egyptian writer who spent more than six years in prison for his political activism has won one of America's biggest literary honours. But Abdelrahman ElGendy could not attend the award ceremony in New York because US officials denied him a visitor visa. ElGendy won the 2026 National Book Award for Nonfiction for his memoir, Huna: A Memoir of Revolution, Prison, and Becoming. The award was announced on November 18 at the 77th National Book Awards ceremony at Cipriani Wall Street in New York.According to Los Angeles Times, ElGendy was absent because the US consular office denied his visitor visa application. He is now living in the United Kingdom after leaving the US in April 2025, fearing that he could be deported to Egypt, where he had previously spent more than six years as a political prisoner.His editor at Hogarth, Helen Thomaides, accepted the award on his behalf and read a statement from the writer. “If you’re listening to this, then a years-long dream of mine has come true, and I’m not there to live it with you,” ElGendy wrote.He recalled imagining, while in his prison cell in Egypt, that he would one day write a memoir about his experiences. He later began hoping that the book might win an award. The recognition came, but he could not be present to receive it.A memoir shaped by revolution and imprisonmentHuna: A Memoir of Revolution, Prison, and Becoming recounts ElGendy's experiences as a political prisoner in Egypt following the country's 2011 revolution. The book explores his imprisonment, personal relationships, family and efforts to rebuild his life.The National Book Foundation's judges described the memoir as a story of survival and resistance. Their citation called it a “lyric testament to survival and resistance” and highlighted the book's account of a father-son relationship built around love, endurance and hope. The book's title draws inspiration from the Arab protest song ‘Sawfa Nabqua Huna,’ which translates as “We Will Remain Here”.In his acceptance statement, ElGendy dedicated the award to people affected by political imprisonment and displacement. He specifically mentioned Palestinians, political prisoners in Egypt and people who have disappeared into US immigration detention.He wrote that he wanted to redirect attention to “the more than 60,000 political prisoners still behind the bars of Egypt’s military dictatorship bankrolled by the U.S. government”. He also referred to “the tens of thousands of souls disappeared in ICE concentration camps”. These were ElGendy's words in his acceptance statement, read at the ceremony by Thomaides.Visa denial became part of the award-night storyThe visa issue had already attracted attention before the ceremony. In an essay for The New Yorker, ElGendy had explained that he could not obtain permission to travel to the US for the event.His absence also became part of the discussion around the 2026 awards. According to Publishers Weekly, Thomaides said the author was “not able to return even as a celebrated visitor and it’s ultimately our loss as a nation”.There was also a separate debate about whether ElGendy met the National Book Award's US residency requirement. As per a New York Times report, his eligibility was questioned because he had left the country. The National Book Foundation defended its decision, explaining that his publisher had confirmed he was a legal and tax-paying US resident who temporarily left in 2025 because he feared for his safety amid immigration arrests.The foundation said it had determined that the information provided met its eligibility rules. The awards had expanded eligibility to non-US citizens in 2024, according to Publishers Weekly.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Percy Jackson returns as teenage stars adapt to the limelight
articles.summary: Percy Jackson's lead Walker Scobell admits there are ups and downs to fame as the series returns.
articles.body:
Percy Jackson is no ordinary teenager - and neither is the actor tasked with bringing the character to life.

As the son of Greek god Poseidon, Percy has demigod status in the hit Disney series and while Walker Scobell doesn't have his powers, that hasn't made the actor's career any less special.

The TV series, based on the novels by Rick Riordan, sets figures from Greek mythology and their children in the modern day and returns on Friday for its third instalment - The Titan's Curse.

Scobell was 14 when he made his debut as Percy in 2023. Now 17, the US actor says growing up in the spotlight has been an adventure in itself.

"There's an upside for each downside," he tells BBC Newsbeat.

"It's a lot easier to get a table at restaurants now and you get to make people's days who are huge Percy Jackson fans just by talking to them for a few minutes. And I think that's a special part of it."

Earlier this year, Scobell posted on Instagram that he would not be attending his school prom because of death threats sent to girls who live near him.

His co-star Aryan Simhadri, who plays Percy's best friend Grover Underwood, has also mentioned uncomfortable meetings with fans.

In an interview with Entertainment Weekly , he spoke about how "about 40 drunk college girls" recognised him and one tried to put her hand in his back pocket.

Since then, he says "fame hasn't been too bad, I've been able to have a normal life because of my parents".

"They really make sure when I'm not filming, I'm grounded and I'm planning for my future instead of being enamoured with the aspects of fame."

The new series is the first time The Titan's Curse has been adapted on screen.

An earlier film adaptation starring Logan Lerman only reached The Sea of Monsters, the second novel in the five-part series.

So the cast say they're in uncharted territory for the project - which sees Percy and Grover trying to rescue Annabeth from Kronos's forces.

"We can make the season in our own weird way because there's nothing you can compare it to, only the book," says Scobell.

"So it's the first time we're seeing any of this stuff."

Fans have been speculating online what to expect, especially after a shock diversion from the novel at the end of the last series.

"I think both book readers and non-book readers are going to be excited and appreciate the tone shift," Simhadri says.

"It changes how serious the world is, it's really the start of a new show, not to be dramatic."

It's caused a split in opinion from the fanbase, with one fan noting "they are going to stick to the books", but another saying "this is a twist they can get down with".

The first series was hugely successful with the opening episode of it reaching 13.3 million viewers, according to entertainment data company Luminate.

That dipped to just over 11 million for the second series and the cast is hoping a fresh take on the story will keep fans interested.

"I personally really like seeing people theorise about what's going to make it," says Simhadri.

"People who have read the books like talking about how they think we're going to adapt it, I love reading those."

It's been a big year for Greek mythology adaptations, with Christopher Nolan's blockbuster The Odyssey getting huge box office numbers and critical acclaim.

Leah Sava Jeffries, who plays Athena's daughter Annabeth Chase, says its popularity could be down to how people connect the ancient stories to their own lives.

"There's stories for everyone," she says.

"You can have a family where the dad is obsessed with The Odyssey but the children are too young, so they can just watch Percy Jackson.

"I feel like there's probably a cooking show about Greek mythology at that point, I mean like there's so many connections no matter what you like."

Percy Jackson is released on Disney+ and Hulu on Friday 20 November.

articles.title: Can the Rohingya genocide verdict deliver justice?
articles.summary: The ICJ has ruled against Myanmar, but safe return, citizenship and reparations remain far from guaranteed.
articles.body:
On Thursday, the International Court of Justice did something it had never done in its 80-year history: It held a state responsible for committing genocide . By nine votes to six, the court found that Myanmar’s 2017 campaign against the Rohingya crossed the gravest threshold in international law.

That matters because Myanmar’s defence was never simply that nothing terrible happened. It argued that its “clearance operations” followed attacks by the Arakan Rohingya Salvation Army (ARSA) and were, however brutal, fundamentally counterterrorism. Genocide requires more than proof of killing, rape or village destruction; it requires specific intent to destroy a protected group.

The court found that Myanmar’s government forces killed thousands of Rohingya civilians, committed widespread sexual violence, inflicted extreme violence on children and attacked people fleeing towards Bangladesh. Taking the evidence together, it concluded that the “only reasonable inference” was an intention to destroy a substantial part of the Rohingya population in northern Rakhine state.

That strips away the central evasion of the past decade. The ARSA attacks were real. So was armed conflict. But rebellion is not a legal alibi for genocide. Nor can the atrocities now be dismissed as excesses by rogue soldiers. This was a judgement about what Myanmar, as a state, did to a people.

The 9-6 split will inevitably be used by Myanmar to cast doubt on the ruling. But the judgement is final and binding. And by 10 votes to five, the court went further, ordering reparations, including safe, voluntary and dignified return, family reunification, restitution of property and compensation where restitution is impossible.

For Rohingya survivors, that is extraordinary vindication. Yasmin Ullah, a Rohingya rights activist who sat in the courtroom, called it “a great day for the Rohingya”. In Cox’s Bazar, refugees had been making an equally practical demand: They want to go home, but with rights, citizenship and dignity .

But here is the problem: You cannot eat a judgement. You cannot live inside one. You cannot rebuild a burned village with one or raise a child safely inside one.

The ICJ has no enforcement arm. Under Article 94(2) of the United Nations Charter, noncompliance can be taken to the UN Security Council (UNSC), where China or Russia could block action. That makes pressure outside the UNSC essential: Targeted sanctions, ASEAN diplomacy, the ICC investigation and Argentina’s universal-jurisdiction case, where arrest warrants have already been issued for 25 suspects.

Who governs the map has also changed. In 2017, Myanmar’s military dominated Rakhine. Today, the Arakan Army controls most of it, and UN investigators have documented forced recruitment, movement restrictions, arbitrary killings and other abuses against Rohingya under its rule.

Any serious return framework must therefore deal with whoever controls the ground. Bangladesh should tie cross-border trade, humanitarian access and political engagement with the Arakan Army to measurable Rohingya benchmarks: Freedom of movement, restoration of land, an end to forced recruitment, international monitoring and a pathway to citizenship. Dhaka should also press Myanmar’s authorities, ASEAN, China, India, Gulf states and Western governments to support a monitored return-and-reparations mechanism. For too long, ports, pipelines and trade corridors have been treated as “strategic” while the Rohingya remain in the humanitarian file.

Everyone wants something from Myanmar. The Rohingya should finally be part of the bill.

None of this matters if the camps fall apart before return becomes possible. About 95 percent of Rohingya refugees are moderately to highly vulnerable and rely almost entirely on humanitarian assistance. The UN’s scaled-down 2026 response plan seeks $710.5m, 26 percent less than the previous year’s appeal. In April, the World Food Programme reduced support for about two-thirds of refugees under a new tiered system; about 17 percent now receive only $7 per person per month.

Donors applauding the verdict should fund the wait as seriously as they praise the destination. The Organisation of Islamic Cooperation, which backed The Gambia’s case, and Gulf donors have a particular responsibility. Western governments should restore cuts, while lenders and donors should support Bangladeshi host communities. Underfunded camps feed trafficking, exploitation and dangerous sea journeys towards Malaysia and Indonesia. A judgement that opens a path home is worth little if the people it was meant for cannot survive the wait.

Reparations now have legal force, not merely moral appeal. Property claims should be documented; land restored where possible; compensation paid where it cannot. Aid says: You are suffering, so we will help you survive. Reparations say: A wrong was done to you, and someone is obliged to repair it.

The verdict is enormous. The test now is simpler: Can the Rohingya go home as citizens, reclaim their land, receive compensation and raise their children somewhere other than a refugee camp?

The court has established the truth. Now justice has to bring it home.

articles.title: 'Food Babe' declares war on the 'holiday death aisle' ahead of Thanksgiving
articles.summary: "Food Babe Feast" author Vani Hari warns families about additives like BHA, BHT and food dyes hiding in packaged stuffing and canned cranberry sauce this Thanksgiving.
articles.body: As Thanksgiving approaches, food activist Vani Hari is targeting the processed ingredients lurking in holiday favorites — and offering a different way to celebrate in her new cookbook. For most Americans, the colorful displays of cookies, candy and seasonal treats greeting shoppers at the supermarket signal that the holidays have arrived. For food activist Vani Hari, better known as the "Food Babe," there is something she considers far more sinister: the "holiday death aisle." 7 COSTCO THANKSGIVING FOOD DEALS AND STEALS THAT SHOPPERS CAN'T MISS THIS HOLIDAY SEASON She's warning families to take a closer look at what's on their holiday tables. "I don't think you need to celebrate the holidays with poison," Hari told Fox News Digital. "You can celebrate the holiday with good, real food." The outspoken food activist is taking on America's holiday eating habits in her new cookbook, "Food Babe Feast: More Than 100 Real Food Recipes for Every Celebration," released this month. Her target isn't just Halloween candy or Christmas cookies. It's an entire food industry she accuses of exploiting nostalgia and convincing Americans that unhealthy indulgences are harmless because they happen only once a year. 8 COMMON FOOD PRESERVATIVES LINKED TO HIGHER RISK OF HIGH BLOOD PRESSURE AND HEART DISEASE "The holiday death aisle is the front of the store — every grocery store, no matter what holiday season it is — where they take over the store with brightly colored treats and concoctions and a lot of different ultra-processed foods that are marketed for that holiday," Hari said. "But I'm telling you, it's not just once a year. It is every month in the grocery store that something's changing." The Washington, D.C.-based National Grocers Association (NGA) pushed back on that characterization. "Seasonal displays are a longstanding retail tradition that help shoppers celebrate holidays and special occasions, but they represent just one part of what local supermarkets offer," an NGA spokesperson said in a statement to Fox News Digital. AMERICANS WHO 'SCREW UP' THEIR EATING SHOULD USE A SIMPLE FIX, SAYS STANFORD SCIENTIST "From fresh produce and locally sourced foods to nutritious options and seasonal favorites, independent grocers provide families with a broad selection of products year-round, while maintaining their everyday focus on delivering quality, value and choice to the communities they serve." Hari argues that even traditional Thanksgiving staples can contain controversial additives, pointing to packaged stuffing, canned cranberry sauce and ingredients commonly used in green bean casserole. Among the substances that Hari urges consumers to avoid are preservatives butylated hydroxyanisole (BHA) and butylated hydroxytoluene (BHT), artificial food dyes and other additives. RFK JR TAKES MAHA TO THE KITCHEN WITH HHS COOKING SERIES PROMOTING HEALTHY MEALS FOR UNDER $5 Her warnings come as federal regulators are taking a fresh look at certain food chemicals. The Food and Drug Administration (FDA) announced reassessments of BHA and BHT in 2026, although those reviews do not establish that foods containing the additives are poisonous or unsafe at permitted levels. Hari, however, said she sees the issue as part of a much bigger problem: a steady stream of heavily processed foods marketed around holidays, birthday parties and other celebrations. "You can have cupcakes, but you need to know what's in them." Her answer is to recreate familiar favorites with ingredients she considers healthier. Instead of canned cranberry sauce sweetened with high-fructose corn syrup, she offers a homemade version sweetened with pineapple. Her cookbook also includes homemade pumpkin spice lattes, peppermint mochas and festive desserts.
