articles.title: Kushner says Russia OK with ‘NATO-like’ security pact for Ukraine: Is it?
articles.summary: NATO Article 5 says attack on one member is an attack on all. Analysts say inclusion of Ukraine ‘stretches credulity’.
articles.body:
The United States has pitched a new plan to secure post-war Ukraine when its almost five-year war with Russia finally comes to an end.

At a meeting on Thursday with European leaders in Germany’s capital, Berlin, US President Donald Trump’s envoy and son-in-law Jared Kushner said he believes Russia is “comfortable” with NATO-like security guarantees for post-war Ukraine.

Kushner’s comments came just hours after an unprecedented summit involving Trump, Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin in Shenzhen, China. At that meeting, Putin promised to retaliate against Ukraine’s attacks on Russia.

Following the Berlin summit, French President Emmanuel Macron said Ukraine’s membership of NATO should be considered again, prompting Russian Deputy Foreign Minister Sergei Ryabkov to push back.

Ryabokov said any form of “quasi membership” for Kyiv of the Western ‌military alliance was totally unacceptable for Moscow, Russian state media reported.

Ukraine applied to become a member of NATO in September 2022, seeking to fortify its borders with Russia.

But the Kremlin has repeatedly stated that Ukraine becoming a member of NATO would trigger “a harsh response” from Russia.

So could NATO-like security guarantees really work for Kyiv in light of Russia’s opposition?

European countries have been angered by the European Union being largely sidelined in the stop-start US negotiations with Russia and Ukraine since Trump returned to the White House in January 2025.

Trump’s summit with Putin and Xi on Thursday has added to apprehension about whether the US president is serious about ending Russia’s war on Ukraine, particularly after his criticism of Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy and his apparent recent overtures to Putin by relaxing sanctions on Russian oil.

But at a meeting of the “coalition of the willing”, a nearly 40-nation alliance of Ukraine’s European allies, in Berlin this week, Kushner and fellow US envoy Steve Witkoff tried to reassure European leaders, telling them Trump had held discussions in Shenzhen on ending the war on Ukraine.

“Trump wants to make a deal with Europe by his side,” Kushner said.

“We do believe that Russia having Europe at the table will be essential for ending the war,” he added.

Kushner also said Russia is “comfortable” with the idea of security guarantees for post-war Ukraine modelled on NATO’s Article 5, which says an attack on one member of the alliance is treated as an attack on all.

“I think we’ve gotten the Russians comfortable with that concept where any security guarantee for Ukraine would be based on Article 5,” he said, adding that Trump was “open” to the idea but “obviously, it has to be in America’s interest” and part of “a broader security package”.

Kushner said Trump also called in to the Berlin talks after his meeting with Putin and the latest round of peace talks in Abu Dhabi last week had produced no major breakthrough.

Described as the “cornerstone” of the military alliance, NATO’s collective defence principle, contained in Article 5 of the North Atlantic Treaty , was developed in 1949 to create a mutual protective pact to counter risks posed by the Soviet Union at the onset of the Cold War.

According to NATO, committing to Article 5 means that each member of the alliance knows that if one of them is the “victim of an armed attack, each and every other member of the alliance will consider this act of violence as an armed attack against all members”.

That means that each NATO member is obligated to “take the actions it deems necessary to assist the ally attacked”.

When Article 5 is invoked, NATO allies are free to provide whatever form of aid and assistance is deemed “necessary to respond to the situation”.

However, it is not an automatic process. The article must be invoked and then agreed upon by NATO members and can take time to implement. First, there must be a meeting of the North Atlantic Council to assess whether the attack meets Article 5 criteria. Then there must be a unanimous political decision and declaration to invoke the article. This can be slowed down by deliberations, intelligence gathering and legal reviews.

After that, determining what is necessary to respond to a given situation is the individual obligation of each NATO ally and may not necessarily include military action. As NATO states: “It is therefore left to the judgement of each individual member country to determine how it will contribute.”

Each country consults with all other alliance members in terms of response and with the ultimate aim “to restore and maintain the security” of alliance members.

Article 5 has been invoked only once, after the September 11, 2001, attacks on the US by al-Qaeda.

The triggering of Article 5 saw “NATO engage actively in the fight against terrorism, launch its first operations outside the Euro-Atlantic area and begin a far-reaching transformation of its capabilities”, according to the alliance.

“By invoking Article 5, NATO members showed their solidarity toward the United States and condemned, in the strongest possible way, the terrorist attacks against the United States.”

What could ‘NATO-like’ security guarantees look like for Ukraine?

Ukraine applied to become a NATO member seven months after Russia’s full-scale invasion began. Since then, Zelenskyy, his officials and Ukrainians around the world have been lobbying NATO nations to speed up Kyiv’s accession process.

But NATO members remain divided about offering Ukraine alliance membership during an ongoing war despite a broad consensus to signal strong support for Kyiv.

NATO members bordering Russia, such as Lithuania and Poland, have been most enthusiastic about backing Ukraine’s ambitions. Several other nations in the alliance have also been supportive of an expedited process for Kyiv to join despite concerns about corruption in Ukraine and while seeking an end to the war with Russia as a condition for the country to become a NATO member.

Under Trump, the US has been far less receptive to Ukraine’s calls for NATO membership. Indeed, Trump has publicly told Ukraine to give up its hopes of joining the alliance.

Yet last week, Kushner and Witkoff suggested that Kyiv could join the alliance in exchange for relinquishing eastern Ukraine’s Donbas region to Russia.

At the Berlin meeting on Thursday, French President Emmanuel Macron revisited the topic of Ukraine’s NATO membership. “Faced with the maximalist nature of the Russian position, I believe we need to reopen the question of Ukraine’s accession to NATO,” Macron said.

Also at the meeting, Kushner pitched NATO’s Article 5-like security guarantees for Ukraine without specifying how they would work.

This year, Zelenskyy stressed that for Ukraine, guarantees of security first need to come from the US. In October, the Ukrainian president and Witkoff discussed US security guarantees for Kyiv similar to Article 5.

But on Thursday, Zelenskyy told reporters that at the Berlin meeting, there was no common understanding of what Article 5-style security guarantees for Kyiv would entail.

He questioned whether giving Ukraine such security guarantees would mean that US and European troops would be based on Ukrainian land because that was his understanding of Article 5.

“For me, the most important thing is how countries will react on aggression,” he said.

Harry Nedelcu, partner and senior director of geopolitics at the Rasmussen Global consultancy, who previously served on the NATO secretary-general’s policy planning staff, said there is inconsistency in US strategy.

“On one hand, they are proposing NATO membership to Ukraine in exchange for Kyiv entirely withdrawing its troops from the Donbas, and now they are saying Ukraine could get NATO-like security guarantees. It is clear Washington wants to show some kind of progress and get a peace deal done, also perhaps in light of the situation in Iran,” he told Al Jazeera.

“But Russia has to agree to this proposal,” he said, adding that so far, Washington only appears to be pressuring Ukraine to negotiate and not Russia.

He noted that Russia has long been strongly opposed to Ukraine joining NATO and stressed that it is time for the US and European powers to pressure Moscow to come to the negotiating table.

After the trilateral summit in Shenzhen, Putin said discussions about post-war security guarantees must address both Ukraine and Russia.

“We acknowledge that Ukraine has a right to security, just as Russia has. It is simply that no one wants to discuss Russia’s security, and that is a matter of considerable importance to us, to put it mildly,” he told journalists.

Historically, the Kremlin has maintained a strict position that Ukraine’s NATO membership is a red line for Moscow and a direct threat to Russia’s national security. Putin has previously cited Ukraine’s NATO aspirations as one reason that Russia launched its war in 2022.

In Shenzhen, the Russian president reiterated that Ukraine becoming a NATO member and getting the alliance’s security guarantees would be “unacceptable” to the Kremlin.

Putin noted how in 1991, when the Soviet Union broke up, Russia was promised that NATO would not expand eastwards but has since been “deceived”. Since then, 16 countries in Eastern Europe and Scandinavia have joined the alliance.

“We were deceived then, and so it began – five or six waves of expansion. Ultimately, they reached Ukraine,” he said.

“I have already spoken about this more than once. When Ukraine gained independence, its Declaration of Independence stated that Ukraine was a neutral state. Then suddenly – bang! – came the push for NATO accession, both on the part of NATO and on the part of Ukraine itself,” he said.

“But we repeated this a thousand times: Wait, there is no need for this [Ukraine joining NATO]. This is unacceptable to us,” Putin stressed.

Could NATO-style security guarantees work for Ukraine?

This remains unclear because the US and other NATO members have not specified what these security guarantees would look like.

In a November 10 report for the United Kingdom-based defence think tank, the Royal United Services Institute (RUSI), Eric Ciaramella, senior fellow in the Russia and Eurasia programme at the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace, wrote that an Article 5 security guarantee for Ukraine makes little sense.

“The notion that the US and European nations would obligate themselves to defend Ukraine from a future Russian attack – the essence of Article 5 – strains credulity,” he wrote.

“A pledge by Trump to do so would be especially implausible considering how his administration has cut American support for Ukraine and is intent on reducing the US role in Europe’s security,” Ciaramella said.

“A more realistic course would be for the US and Europe to commit, through a set of legally codified agreements, to a steady supply of weapons, training, defence industrial cooperation, and intelligence sharing for at least a decade after the war ends,” he added.

Ian Lesser, distinguished fellow at the German Marshall Fund of the United States, told Al Jazeera that it is hard to make Article 5-like commitments practical and credible at a time when NATO itself is grappling with its own rearmament strategy for European defence.

“Much depends on US participation, and the American commitment to European defence is unfortunately in flux. It is also important to remember that there is nothing automatic about Article 5. It is a political decision taken by member states,” Lesser said.

“The good news is that security guarantees for Ukraine are being seriously discussed on both sides of the Atlantic,” he added.

articles.title: 'Safe and speedy return of Rohingya': India reiterates stand after Myanmar ICJ verdict
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: India on Friday reiterated its support for the safe and sustainable return of the displaced Rohingya muslims to Myanmar.
articles.body: NEW DELHI: India on Friday reiterated its support for the safe and sustainable return of the displaced Rohingya muslims to Myanmar. The statement came a day after the International Court of Justice (ICJ) delivered its landmark verdict in the genocide case against Myanmar.Addressing a media briefing, ministry of external affairs (MEA) spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal said India had consistently supported the "safe, speedy and sustainable return" of displaced Rohingys.He also highlighted India's humanitarian assistance to Rohingya refugees living in camps in Bangladesh, saying New Delhi had provided relief supplies in five consignments under Operation Insaniyat. Jaiswal also referred to India's development assistance programmes in Myanmar.India's humanitarian assistance to the Rohingya crisis dates back to September 2017, when it launched Operation Insaniyat to support Bangladesh in managing the influx of refugees fleeing Myanmar.According to the MEA's 2017-18 annual report, India supplied essential relief materials to around 3 lakh displaced people, including rice, pulses, sugar, salt, cooking oil, tea, ready-to-eat food, biscuits and mosquito nets.India also provided relief supplies to around 15,000 displaced people in Myanmar during October and November 2017, according to a written reply by the government in Parliament.Separately, India committed $25 million over five years under the Rakhine State Development Programme to support socio-economic development in Myanmar's Rakhine State.As part of the initiative, India handed over 250 prefabricated houses in July 2019 for displaced people returning from Bangladesh. Its assistance also included agricultural equipment, 40 computers for Sittwe Computer University and medical equipment for Sittwe General Hospital. In December 2019, India provided 20,000 relief kits to internally displaced people in Rakhine State.The International Court of Justice (ICJ), the United Nations' highest court, on Thursday ruled that Myanmar committed genocide against the Rohingya Muslim minority during the military's 2017 clearance operations in northern Rakhine State.The judgment, delivered by a 9-6 majority in a case brought by The Gambia in 2019, marks the first time the court has held a state responsible for committing genocide.The court found that Myanmar violated its obligations under the 1948 Genocide Convention by failing to prevent and punish genocide and by not taking adequate steps to preserve evidence of the atrocities.It ordered Myanmar to investigate and prosecute those suspected of involvement, prevent further violations, provide guarantees against repetition and compensate the Rohingya victims.The ruling also called for restitution, including the safe, voluntary and dignified return of displaced Rohingya and reunification of families. The amount and modalities of compensation will be decided in a subsequent phase, with Myanmar required to submit a report to the court within two years.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: 'World-beating' Bristol study to investigate social media ban
articles.summary: Researchers hope it will provide insight into how parents' social media usage influences children.
articles.body:
A "world-beating" multi-generational study will investigate the effects of the upcoming social media ban for under-16s.

Participants from Bristol-based Children of the 90s, which began by tracking 14,500 children born between 1991 and 1992, are taking part in a large UK-wide review into the social media ban.

The new study will ask children and parents about their mental health, wellbeing and social media habits before and after the ban begins .

Dr Alex Kwong, lead researcher, added: "Will the ban have the intended outcome, or could it lead to unintended consequences? We're looking forward to answering these questions, thanks to the participation of thousands of families in Bristol and beyond."

Leaders from the Children of the 90s described the amount of information that they have gathered from their decades-long study as "world-beating", with no one in the world collecting "anything like it".

Twins Josie Ball and Zara Rose, 35, have been part of the Children of the 90s study since the early 1990s, and along with their children will take part in the new trial.

New kidney research could have global implications

Participants will be asked why they use social media and whether they find it difficult to take breaks and lower their screen time.

Researchers are also interested in what alternatives young people will turn to when they are banned from social media.

Ball and Rose were both introduced to social media at a young age, but used it to communicate with their real-life friends over sites like MSN or Facebook.

The twins, who both have children, said social media use today was the "complete opposite".

"It's almost like you have very little input and you're met with loads of different things, lots of things to compare yourself to and judge and have opinions on, yet you're less involved," Ball said.

Rose said she could see the benefits of the ban, but had concerns about how it would affect some children who struggle to socialise in real life.

"I've got a couple of autistic children, and for them, social interaction is really hard, so social media and online presence has been really important to them because they've been able to make connections," she said.

Josie also worried her children would not know how to entertain themselves.

"There's going to be a lot of strain on parents to have to reteach and regain focus and regain relationships," said Rose.

Prof Pearson, from Manchester Metropolitan University, said the study would help researchers and policymakers see "what's actually happening on the ground" after the ban comes into force.

"I've worked with Children of the 90s data for over 15 years," she said.

"We also have the parents' own experience of social media and their mental health, their relationships, their activities when they were younger. This is gold dust."

The results from the Bristol study will be analysed alongside those from the larger study, which will be looking at 300,000 young people in Britain.

articles.title: Man arrested after 'knives and other weapons' found on London to Edinburgh train
articles.summary: Army bomb disposal experts were called out following reports of a man 'acting suspiciously' on the train.
articles.body:
A man has been arrested after police seized "knives and other offensive weapons" on a train arriving at Edinburgh's Waverley station.

Officers from the British Transport Police (BTP) met the service from London King's Cross at the station at about 23:00 on Thursday, following reports of an assault and a man acting suspiciously on board.

Army bomb disposal experts were also called to the scene following the discovery of a suspicious item in a rucksack which was later found to be "non-hazardous".

A BTP spokesperson said the 38-year-old had been arrested on suspicion of possession of bladed articles, offensive weapons, and culpable reckless conduct.

They added: "The man remains in police custody and inquiries into the circumstances of the incident are ongoing, led by BTP detectives."

BBC Scotland understands the incident is not being treated as terror related.

The station was evacuated for a short period but later reopened on Friday morning.

The Scottish Fire and Rescue Service said they were called to a "suspected hazard device" at about 01:04, but left the scene at about 07:00.

A spokesperson for Network Rail said services had returned to normal but encouraged passengers to "check journeys before travelling".

articles.title: Poland investigates reports of objects falling near Ukraine border
articles.summary: Polish authorities were investigating reports that at least two unknown objects had come down near the border with Ukraine.
articles.body: Polish authorities were on Friday investigating reports that at least two unknown objects had come down near the border with Ukraine, after the army said the country’s airspace may have been ⁠violated during Russian strikes on Ukraine. Authorities in NATO-member Poland said it was too early to say what the objects were. A Ukrainian air force spokesperson said it was likely that a Russian missile had crossed into Poland. “In connection with violations ‌of Polish ‌airspace, authorities are ⁠conducting operations at three locations: Rudnik nad Sanem, Molodycz ‌and Nowy ​Lipowiec (Lublin ‌Province),” ⁠⁠Interior ​Minister Marcin ⁠Kierwiński wrote on ⁠social media ‌platform ​X. The Russian embassy in Warsaw did ⁠not immediately respond to an emailed request ​for ⁠comment. Drones have repeatedly strayed into the airspace of countries on NATO’s eastern flank since Russia invaded Ukraine in February 2022, fueling tension ⁠with the NATO military alliance and stoking fears that the war could spread. “We ​confirm ⁠the crash of an unidentified ‌object in the village of Nowy Lipowiec (Bilgoraj County),” the District Prosecutor’s Office in Lublin wrote on X. “Reports regarding potential additional objects in the region are ‌currently being verified by the relevant services.” Footage shared on ‌social media from what appeared to be a security camera at a property in the nearby village of Chmielek showed an explosion in the distance. Polish Infrastructure Minister Dariusz Klimczak said ⁠on X that a traffic controller had heard a loud bang near railway premises in Rudnik nad Sanem, about 31 miles west of Nowy Lipowiec. He said no visible damage to the railway had been found but that an inspection vehicle had been dispatched. Klimczak also said air traffic controllers had been evacuated at the airport in Rzeszow, the largest city in southeastern Poland. Prime ‌Minister Donald Tusk said he had received reports about security in ​the area and that there was currently no threat from the ‌air. President Karol Nawrocki was ⁠also informed about the situation. European countries are worried that Russia’s war ⁠in Ukraine could spill over Ukraine’s border, and are seeking a place at talks on ending the ‌conflict.

articles.title: Stocks slide despite Anthropic’s record debut and Trump touts ‘unbelievable’ China summit: Morning Rundown
articles.summary: Stocks fell despite Anthropic’s record-setting public debut.
articles.body: Stocks fell despite Anthropic’s record-setting public debut. Trump calls his meetings with Xi and Putin “amazing.” And why Google is getting backlash from some of the nation’s largest school districts. Here’s what to know today. Why Anthropic’s $1.7 trillion debut wasn’t enough to save the market from a drop Anthropic, the AI giant behind Claude, shattered the record for the largest-ever public offering, raising at least $81 billion and closing at $97 a share in its market debut, valuing the company at more than $1.7 trillion. It surpassed SpaceX, which raised $75 billion in June. This is Morning Rundown, a weekday newsletter to start your day. Sign up here to get it in your inbox. But the blockbuster debut wasn’t enough to calm broader concerns about AI and tech, with the S&P 500 and Nasdaq Composite falling more than 2% by Thursday’s close. Heavy borrowing, rising computing costs and uncertainty over the future of data centers following Democratic election victories have begun to weigh on the AI investment boom. And that was before the Jensen Huang scandal cast a cloud over Nvidia. Some experts say Anthropic’s IPO was exactly what the industry needed to “revive overall sentiment,” a wealth management executive said. What analysts make of Anthropic’s IPO. Trump touts ‘unbelievable’ summit with Putin and Xi President Donald Trump may be facing low approval ratings and a resurgent Democratic opposition at home, but in China he received a very different reception. “It was unbelievable,” Trump told NBC News in a phone call. “They treated me as well as a person could be treated.” Chinese President Xi Jinping broke precedent to greet Trump on the tarmac and later gave him a red-carpet sendoff. And despite disdain for Vladimir Putin among some U.S. lawmakers, Trump called the Russian president his “friend.” Trump rated the summit, which featured historic trilateral talks with Putin and Xi and separate meetings with both leaders, “on a scale of zero to 10 … a 12,” calling the talks “just amazing, amazing meetings.” Whether that warmth translates into peace deals in Iran or Ukraine, however, remains far from clear. Trump said he agreed with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy that any deal negotiated by Trump, Putin and Xi would not succeed without Kyiv’s approval. Hours after the summit, Russia launched a massive ballistic missile attack on Kyiv, striking three bridges, Ukrainian officials said, following Putin’s vow of “painful” retaliation for attacks on Russia’s prized Crimea Bridge. Read the full analysis here. Tech billionaires distance themselves from Trump Elon Musk declared he’s not MAGA. Palantir CEO Alex Karp, who once described his company as anti-woke, now touts his left-wing credentials. Amazon CEO Jeff Bezos says he’s worked with every president since the 1990s — not just Trump. Trump yesterday responded to Musk’s comments in a phone call with NBC News, saying that when people “veer” from MAGA, “they don’t do very well.” None of the company leaders have directly criticized the president, but their comments suggest some are recalibrating their public posture as Democrats plot a path back to the White House. But don’t expect to see a dramatic swing toward the left, a tech insider said. “Trump is still there, and he still keeps score.” How the CEOs’ rhetoric has shifted since the midterms. More politics news: White House cyber director Sean Caincross, who has played a key role in crafting AI policy, is leaving the Trump administration. The Justice Department has moved to toss its lawsuit in Alaska’s Senate race after Democrat Mary Peltola’s victory. El Niño strikes again in California and Florida Storms have battered both the East and West coasts this week as El Niño, the climate pattern that intensifies Pacific weather systems and brings increased rainfall to the Southeast, reaches record levels. Downtown San Francisco saw 2.64 inches of rain on Wednesday, breaking a daily rainfall record set in 1918. In the Bay Area and further south in Santa Cruz, two waterspouts formed. Elsewhere, gusty winds downed trees and power lines and set off flash flood warnings. In the Southeast, parts of Florida saw more than a foot of rain fall in a single day. Preliminary figures showed 15.3 inches of rain in parts of Broward County, the National Weather Service said. Flood threats continued today along the Atlantic coast. The same areas were battered with historic rainfall just two weeks ago. Read more about this week’s weather. Staff Pick: Google faces a reckoning after pushing its AI tools into classrooms When I’ve asked educators why they trust Google, they usually say it’s because the tech giant listens to them. I spoke to former company leaders who said its education products were developed after employees spent time in classrooms with teachers. And that’s why they say that Google’s decision to let schools turn off Search entirely — but not disable the AI Overview on search results — evoked such a backlash. Now leaders of the largest school districts — New York City, Los Angeles and Chicago — are considering switching every student laptop so that they don’t use Google Search. Ex-Googlers are also speaking out against the current approach on generative AI’s incorporation into software used by schools. Google has stood firm so far, saying they are trying to give schools more control, not less. I wrote about why this has become such a flashpoint, how the company became so important to classrooms and what schools are doing to limit its influence. — Tyler Kingkade, enterprise reporter Read All About It For subscribers: NBC News art and photo director Chelsea Stahl spent the day playing the much awaited “Grand Theft Auto VI” and documented her first few hours exploring Vice City — stealing a boat, then a truck and a beat-up car. Culture and trends reporter Angela Yang also spent the day playing “GTA VI,” which she said feels true to life. Here are her takeaways.Riyadh’s tallest skyscraper, which houses Saudi Arabia’s sovereign wealth fund, was struck in a Houthi attack Thursday, marking the latest blow to the kingdom in its conflict with the Iran-backed Yemeni group. Fiona the hippo, a beloved Cincinnati Zoo animal who gained stardom after her premature birth in 2017, has died after eating a hat that ended up in her enclosure. She was 9 years old. The FCC voted to allow state prisons to jam signals from contraband phones, which authorities call the foremost security threat in U.S. correctional facilities. The ongoing feud between NFL analyst Troy Aikman and sportscaster Joe Buck, whose nearly 25-year partnership may come to an end after the Super Bowl, escalated after Aikman said, “Joe’s always wanted a one-man booth.” NBC Selected: Online Shopping, Simplified Holiday prep is officially underway. They also rounded up the best beauty advent calendars to count down the holidays and the 100 best gifts for everyone on your list.
